# DISEÑO EXPERIMENTAL COMPLETO
## Pregunta: ¿Aumentar el tamaño de un modelo necesariamente mejora el rendimiento, o pueden insuficiencias en pre-entrenamiento y alineación negar sus beneficios?

---

## A. RATIONALE DETALLADO

### A.1 Motivación Científica
La pregunta aborda una tensión fundamental en escalado de LLMs:
- **Ley de escalado (positivo)**: Mayor tamaño → mayor capacidad → mejor rendimiento (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022)
- **Contrapunto empírico**: Rendimiento depende también de cantidad y calidad de pre-entrenamiento, además de alineación post-entrenamiento (Touvron et al., 2023 - Llama-2 paper)

Tu pregunta implica que **dos factores podrían "cancelar" la ventaja de tamaño**:
1. **Pre-entrenamiento insuficiente**: Volumen inadecuado de tokens de pre-entrenamiento relativo al tamaño
2. **Alineación refinada débil**: Falta de RLHF/instruction-tuning que desbloquee el potencial real del modelo

### A.2 Diseño para Aislar Efectos
Usamos un diseño factorial 2×2 que permite descomponer:
- **Efecto principal de tamaño**: (70B) - (13B) en iguales condiciones de entrenamiento
- **Efecto principal de alineación**: (Chat) - (Base) en igual tamaño
- **Interacción**: ¿La alineación beneficia más al 70B o al 13B?

### A.3 Operacionalización de Conceptos
| Concepto | Operacionalización |
|----------|-------------------|
| **Pre-entrenamiento insuficiente** | Análisis teórico vs. Chinchilla scaling law + comparación 70B-base vs. 13B-chat |
| **Alineación refinada** | Variantes Chat (RLHF) vs. Base (solo pre-entrenamiento) |
| **Mejora en rendimiento** | Cambio en accuracy/score en benchmarks multidimensionales |
| **Alineación de calidad** | TruthfulQA, XSTEST, BBQ (miden honestidad, robustez, sesgo) |

---

## B. CONDICIONES Y CONTROLES

### B.1 Matriz Experimental (4 Condiciones)

```
                     BASE (No RLHF)        CHAT (RLHF-aligned)
13B parámetros    [1] Llama-2-13B        [2] Llama-2-13B-Chat
70B parámetros    [3] Llama-2-70B        [4] Llama-2-70B-Chat
```

**Razón de 4 condiciones**: Permite 6 comparaciones pareadas (ver sección D.2)

### B.2 Condiciones Controladas (Fijas para todas)

| Parámetro | Valor | Justificación |
|-----------|-------|---------------|
| **Temperatura** | 0.7 | Estándar para evaluación; balancea coherencia y variación |
| **Max tokens** | 2048 | Suficiente para respuestas complejas; constante entre modelos |
| **Top-p (nucleus sampling)** | 0.95 | Estándar en benchmarks; reduce cherry-picking de respuestas |
| **Context window** | 4096 o disponible máximo | Igual para ambos tamaños |
| **Versión de modelos** | Llama-2 oficial (Meta, Jul 2023) | Reproducibilidad; no versiones posteriores mejoradas |
| **Prompts** | Idénticos para todas las condiciones | Control de variable confundente |
| **Número de runs** | 3-5 por ejemplo (si se ejecuta) | Capturar variabilidad; media de resultados |

### B.3 Variables Medidas (Independientes)

1. **Tamaño**: Fijo en 13B vs. 70B (5.4x diferencia)
2. **Tipo de entrenamiento**: Fijo en Base vs. Chat

---

## C. SELECCIÓN DE BENCHMARKS CON JUSTIFICACIÓN

### C.1 Estructura Multidimensional

Los benchmarks se organizan en **3 dimensiones** que responden a aspectos distintos de la pregunta:

#### **Dimensión 1: Capacidad Base (Rendimiento Cognitivo Puro)**
Mide si el tamaño confiere ventaja en razonamiento general, independiente de alineación.

| Benchmark | Métrica | Qué mide | Justificación |
|-----------|---------|----------|---------------|
| **MMLU** | Accuracy (%) | Razonamiento multidominio: STEM, humanidades, social sciences | Estándar de oro en evaluación LLM; 57 subcategorías; 14k ejemplos |
| **HellaSwag** | Accuracy (%) | Sentido común (next event prediction) | Complementa MMLU; requiere comprensión causal y secuencial |
| **ARC (Challenge)** | Accuracy (%) | Razonamiento científico de grado escolar | Más difícil que ARC-Easy; discrimina bien entre modelos |

**Interpretación**:
- Si 70B > 13B significativamente aquí: Tamaño confiere ventaja cognitiva
- Si 70B-base < 13B-chat aquí: Alineación puede compensar tamaño en tarea cognitiva

#### **Dimensión 2: Alineación y Seguridad**
Mide si la variante Chat captura genuinamente "mejor alineación" y si esta suaviza o acentúa diferencias de tamaño.

| Benchmark | Métrica | Qué mide | Justificación |
|-----------|---------|----------|---------------|
| **TruthfulQA** | Accuracy (%) | Honestidad: evita información falsa al responder preguntas engañosas | Métrica de "alineación sincera"; captura si modelo prefiere admitir no-saber |
| **XSTEST** | Refusal rate (%) | Robustez: correctamente rehúsa peticiones adversariales | Mide si modelo mantiene límites de seguridad bajo presión |
| **BBQ (Bias)** | Bias score (%) | Sesgos en demografía/estereotipos | Alineación incluye equidad; mide si Chat reduce sesgos vs. Base |

**Interpretación**:
- Si Chat >> Base en estas métricas: Alineación es real y medible
- Si 70B-chat ~ 13B-chat: Tamaño no afecta significativamente alineación (hipótesis de ceiling effect)
- Si 70B-base >> 13B-base: Tamaño puede amplificar comportamientos no alineados (¿emergencia de capacidades problemáticas?)

#### **Dimensión 3: Capacidades Especializadas**
Mide si el tamaño permite mejores capacidades técnicas y si alineación las preserva/daña.

| Benchmark | Métrica | Qué mide | Justificación |
|-----------|---------|----------|---------------|
| **HumanEval** | Pass@1 (%) | Generación de código correcto | Tarea especializada donde tamaño típicamente ayuda mucho |
| **SQuAD 2.0** | F1/EM (%) | Comprensión lectora y reconocimiento de no-respuesta | Mide si alineación (Chat) degrada velocidad de respuesta vs. Base |

**Interpretación**:
- Si 70B >> 13B en HumanEval: Tamaño crítico para especialización
- Si Chat << Base en SQuAD EM: RLHF introduce "cautela" que daña tareas específicas
- Si diferencias pequeñas: Tamaño y alineación desacoplados en estas tareas

---

## D. PLAN DE ANÁLISIS

### D.1 Matriz de Comparaciones Clave

Las 4 condiciones permiten 6 comparaciones pareadas. **Priorizamos 4**:

| # | Comparación | Hipótesis que responde | Resultado esperado si H₁ (tamaño) | Resultado esperado si H₂ (alineación) |
|----|-----------|----------------------|--------------------------------|--------------------------------|
| **⭐ A** | 70B-chat vs. 13B-chat | ¿Tamaño mejora cuando está alineado? | 70B-chat >> 13B-chat | Diferencia pequeña (~5% o menos) |
| **⭐ B** | 70B-base vs. 13B-base | ¿Tamaño mejora sin alineación? | 70B-base > 13B-base | 70B-base < 13B-base en alineación-metrics |
| **🔥 CRÍTICA** | 70B-base vs. 13B-chat | **¿Tamaño puede compensar falta de alineación?** | **70B-base ≥ 13B-chat en capacidad base** | **70B-base << 13B-chat en alineación-metrics** |
| **D** | Chat effect (70B) vs. Chat effect (13B) | ¿Alineación beneficia igual a ambos? | Ambos se benefician ~igual | 70B se beneficia más |

**Interpretación de la comparación CRÍTICA (70B-base vs. 13B-chat)**:
- **Responde directamente tu pregunta**: ¿Puede tamaño desnudo (sin alineación) vencer alineación en modelo pequeño?

| Escenario | Resultado | Interpretación |
|-----------|-----------|-----------------|
| **A: 70B-base >> 13B-chat en capacidad base** | Tamaño domina (H₁ correcta) | Más parámetros > alineación refinada |
| **B: 70B-base ≈ 13B-chat en capacidad base** | Empate (trade-off) | Ambos factores igualmente importantes |
| **C: 70B-base < 13B-chat en capacidad base** | Alineación domina (H₂ correcta) | Alineación refinada + instrucciones superan tamaño bruto |
| **D: 70B-base > 13B-chat en capacidad base, pero << en alineación-metrics** | Especialización vs. seguridad | Modelo grande y no alineado: mejor en tareas, peor en robustez |

### D.2 Análisis Estadístico

#### **Métricas de Diferencia**

Para cada benchmark, calcular:

1. **Diferencia Absoluta**: Δ = Modelo_A - Modelo_B
   - Ejemplo: TruthfulQA(70B-chat) - TruthfulQA(13B-chat) = +8.3 puntos

2. **Diferencia Relativa (%)**: (Δ / Baseline) × 100
   - Baseline = 13B-chat (modelo "más justo" con alineación)
   - Ejemplo: (8.3 / 45.2) × 100 = 18.4% mejora

3. **Efecto de Tamaño (ΔSize)**:
   - ΔSize = [Promedio(70B) - Promedio(13B)] / Promedio(13B)
   - Se calcula sobre TODAS las condiciones

4. **Efecto de Alineación (ΔAlign)**:
   - ΔAlign = [Promedio(Chat) - Promedio(Base)] / Promedio(Base)
   - Se calcula sobre AMBOS tamaños

#### **Umbrales de Significancia Sustantiva**

Dado que usamos benchmarks estándar con scores reportados (no hay incertidumbre estadística tradicional), usamos **umbrales de significancia sustantiva**:

| Diferencia | Interpretación |
|-----------|-----------------|
| < 2% | Negligible; no afecta conclusión |
| 2-5% | Pequeña; mencionable pero no decisiva |
| 5-10% | Moderada; importante para conclusión |
| > 10% | Grande; reversa conclusiones tipicas |

**Justificación**: MMLU típicamente distingue modelos con 3-5% de diferencia.

#### **Análisis Interactivo**

Crear tabla de "ganancia marginal":
```
Ganancia relativa de pasar de 13B→70B, según alineación:

                  CAPACIDAD BASE (MMLU)     ALINEACIÓN (TruthfulQA)
Base→70B:         +12% (efecto tamaño puro)    +3% (tamaño sin alineación)
Chat→70B:         +8% (tamaño + alineación)    +2% (alineación ya buena)

Interpretación:
- Tamaño más beneficioso cuando NO hay alineación (+12% vs. +8%)
- Alineación "satura" con tamaño: 70B-chat no mucho mejor que 13B-chat en honestidad
```

### D.3 Síntesis de Hallazgos

Tabla resumen de 3×3 para cada dimensión:

```
DIMENSIÓN 1: CAPACIDAD BASE
                    13B-Base    70B-Base    13B-Chat    70B-Chat
MMLU                42.5%       50.2%       53.1%       58.9%
HellaSwag           79.1%       84.6%       85.2%       88.3%
ARC-Challenge       56.3%       62.4%       65.1%       68.7%

Patrón esperado si H₁ (tamaño domina):
- 70B >> 13B en todas filas
- Chat marginal vs. tamaño

Patrón esperado si H₂ (alineación domina):
- Chat >> Base en todas filas
- Tamaño marginal dado alineación buena
```

---

## E. FACTIBILIDAD

### E.1 Recursos Necesarios para Ejecución

| Recurso | Requerimiento | Opciones disponibles |
|---------|---------------|---------------------|
| **Hardware** | GPU VRAM | Llama-2-70B: ~140GB VRAM (8×A100 o equivalente) / Llama-2-13B: ~26GB VRAM (1×A100) |
| **Alternativa** | CPU inference | Posible con cuantización (4-bit): reduce a ~35GB (70B), ~7GB (13B); más lento |
| **Acceso a modelos** | Pesos Llama-2 | ✅ Disponibles públicamente (HuggingFace, Meta) |
| **Tiempo de ejecución** | Por benchmark | MMLU: ~2 horas (70B), ~30 min (13B); TruthfulQA: ~4 horas (70B) |
| **Costo** | Si cloud | ~$50-200 USD si usas AWS/GCP (8×A100 GPU) por 48 horas; o ~$0 si acceso académico |

### E.2 Viabilidad de Ejecución Completa

**Escenario 1: Acceso a GPU (Recomendado)**
- Timeline: 3-5 días para pipeline completo (inference + evaluación)
- Costo: $100-300 (si cloud) o $0 (institución académica)
- ✅ **VIABLE** con recursos estándar (clusters académicos disponibles)

**Escenario 2: Sin GPU (CPU inference)**
- Timeline: 2-4 semanas (cuantización + inference lento)
- Costo: $0 si local, o ~$30 si cloud CPU
- ⚠️ **VIABLE pero NO RECOMENDADO** (muy lento)

**Escenario 3: Benchmarks Reportados (Recomendado para este diseño)**
- Timeline: 1-2 días (compilar scores publicados en Meta paper + otros)
- Costo: $0 (solo literatura)
- ✅ **ÓPTIMO PARA ESTE DISEÑO-ONLY** (ya hay reportes reproducibles de Meta, papers de benchmarks)

### E.3 Fuentes de Datos Recomendadas

Para ejecutar sin GPU (compile scores published):

- Llama-2-13B: 2.0 Billones tokens
- Llama-2-70B: 2.0 Billones tokens

- **13B está "sobrecapacitado" en tokens** (Meta invirtió más pre-entrenamiento del óptimo)
- **70B está más cerca del óptimo** (Meta ajustó mejor la relación tamaño-tokens para 70B)
- **Conclusión**: Ambos fueron pre-entrenados *suficientemente*, pero **el 70B está mejor balanceado**

**Insight teórico para incluir en discusión**:
- No es que 70B sea "insuficientemente pre-entrenado" en términos absolutos
- Sino que **ambos modelos tienen tokens_used/tokens_optimal diferente**
- Esta diferencia en "eficiencia de tokens" es un **mecanismo plausible** por el que 70B podría superar al 13B

**Cómo se usa en análisis**:

## Proposed Experiment Design: Pipeline Parallelism Throughput Analysis

### Research Question
Does throughput for 1F1B, 1F1B-I, and ZB-1p improve as microbatches increase, while ZB-2p maintains high throughput with fewer microbatches?

### Experiment Design Overview

**Objective**: Compare throughput behavior across four scheduling methods as a function of microbatch count, validating the hypothesis that ZB-2p achieves superior efficiency at low microbatch counts.

**Primary Metric**: Throughput (samples/second or tokens/second)

**Independent Variable**: Number of microbatches (M) = {1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64}

**Dependent Variables**: 
- Throughput (primary)
- Pipeline utilization (% time without bubbles)
- Memory peak usage per stage
- Total iteration time

**Methods Under Test**: 1F1B, 1F1B-I, ZB-1p, ZB-2p

### Experimental Configuration (Fixed Parameters)

**Model & Task**:
- Model: Transformer-based language model (~1-7B parameters)
- Task: Language model training (forward + backward passes)
- Global batch size: Fixed at 64-128 samples per iteration
- Sequence length: Fixed (e.g., 2048 tokens)

**Hardware Configuration**:
- Pipeline depth (P): 4-8 stages (GPU devices or simulated stages)
- Device type: GPU (V100/A100 typical; CPU-only feasible for validation)
- Synchronization: Synchronous pipeline (bounded staleness)

**Hyperparameters**:
- Learning rate, optimizer: Fixed across all methods
- Gradient accumulation steps: Tied to microbatch count (M)
- Iterations per trial: ≥100 for stable throughput estimates

### Methodology

**1. Controlled Comparison Setup**
- For each method (1F1B, 1F1B-I, ZB-1p, ZB-2p):
  - Initialize identical model weights (checkpoint-based seeding)
  - Run ≥3 independent trials per (method, M) pair
  - Exclude first 5-10 iterations (warmup) to avoid initialization overhead

**2. Throughput Measurement**
- Record: (total_samples_processed, wall_clock_time) for iterations 10 through N
- Calculate: throughput = total_samples / wall_clock_time
- Report: mean ± std across trials

**3. Expected Outcomes** (Hypothesis Validation)
- **1F1B, 1F1B-I, ZB-1p**: Throughput increases with M (diminishing returns after M≈8-16)
- **ZB-2p**: Throughput plateaus early (M≥2-4), indicating robustness to low microbatch counts
- **Relative improvement**: ZB-2p achieves ≥90% peak throughput at M=4; others require M≥8

**4. Controls & Baselines**
- Baseline: Single-GPU training (no pipeline) as throughput ceiling
- Control: Sequential pipeline (1F1B with M=1) as worst-case lower bound
- Sanity check: Verify all methods produce identical loss curves (correctness validation)

**5. Secondary Measurements**
- Pipeline bubble percentage: (idle_cycles / total_cycles) per stage
- Gradient staleness: Maximum backward propagation delay relative to forward pass
- Memory utilization: Peak memory per stage (detect OOM at high M)

### Key Assumptions

1. Four methods are implemented or can be simulated in a common framework
2. Model is transformer-based with regular layer structure suitable for pipelining
3. Throughput is measured in samples/second (or tokens/second for NLP tasks)
4. All methods perform synchronous gradient updates (same loss convergence behavior)
5. Pipeline has 4-8 stages; GPU or CPU-based execution is feasible
6. Microbatch count can be varied independently from global batch size
7. Method implementations are functionally correct (gradients converge identically)

### Consequential Uncertainties

1. **Throughput metric definition**: Samples/sec vs tokens/sec vs iterations/sec; clarify in implementation
2. **Memory constraints**: May limit maximum feasible microbatch count per method
3. **Hardware scaling**: Results may not generalize across different pipeline depths (P=4 vs P=16)
4. **Implementation parity**: Whether all methods use identical communication and computation kernels
5. **Gradient staleness impact**: Whether ZB methods trade convergence speed for throughput
6. **Optimal M identification**: Whether saturation point (M*) is data/model-dependent

### Validation Checks

1. **Correctness**: Verify loss curves are identical ± numerical precision across methods
2. **Monotonicity**: Check if 1F1B throughput is monotonically non-decreasing with M (within error bars)
3. **Saturation**: Identify M* where throughput plateaus (<2% improvement for ΔM=2) for each method
4. **Ranking consistency**: Confirm ZB-2p > ZB-1p ≥ 1F1B-I > 1F1B at low M

### Expected Artifacts

- Throughput vs. microbatch count plot (4 curves with error bars)
- Pipeline utilization heatmap (method × M)
- Memory consumption table
- Summary table: (method, M, throughput, bubble%, peak_memory)

# Complete Experiment Design: Pipeline Parallelism Throughput Analysis

## Research Question
**Does throughput for methods 1F1B, 1F1B-I, and ZB-1p improve as the number of microbatches increases, while ZB-2p maintains high throughput even with fewer microbatches?**

---

## 1. REPOSITORY GROUNDING

### 1.1 Code Structure & Method Parameterization

The design assumes a pipeline parallelism framework (likely modeled on ZeroBubble, PipeDream, or GPipe implementations) with the following structure:

**Expected File Organization:**
- `scheduler/` or `scheduling/` directory containing method implementations
  - `1f1b.py` - One-Forward-One-Backward scheduling
  - `1f1b_interleaved.py` - Interleaved 1F1B variant
  - `zb_1pass.py` - ZeroBubble single-pass variant
  - `zb_2pass.py` - ZeroBubble two-pass variant
- `trainer.py` or `train.py` - Main training loop that selects and executes scheduling methods
- `config.py` or `config/` - Configuration management for method selection and parameters
- `utils/profiling.py` or `metrics/` - Throughput measurement and logging utilities
- `benchmarks/` or `experiments/` - Pre-existing benchmarking scripts

**Expected Parameterization Methods:**

1. **Command-line arguments** (most common):
   - `--schedule-method {1f1b | 1f1b_interleaved | zb_1pass | zb_2pass}`
   - `--num-microbatches M` (integer, ranging 1-64)
   - `--microbatch-size` (samples per microbatch; typically fixed)
   - `--num-stages` or `--pipeline-depth` (number of pipeline stages)
   - `--num-iterations` (iterations for throughput measurement)
   - `--warmup-iterations` (typically 5-10, excluded from throughput calculation)

2. **Config files** (if present):
   - YAML or JSON config with keys like:
     ```yaml
     scheduling:
       method: "zb_2pass"
       num_microbatches: 8
       microbatch_size: 32  # FIXED
       num_stages: 4
     measurement:
       warmup_iterations: 10
       benchmark_iterations: 100
       measure_memory: true
       measure_bubbles: true
     ```

3. **Environment variables** (less common but sometimes used):
   - `PIPELINE_METHOD`, `NUM_MICROBATCHES`, etc.

### 1.2 Existing Throughput Measurement Utilities

Look for existing implementations in:
- `utils/metrics.py` or `profiling/throughput.py` with functions like:
  - `measure_throughput(num_samples, wall_time) → samples/sec`
  - `calculate_pipeline_utilization() → bubble_percentage`
  - `measure_peak_memory() → bytes_per_stage`
- Logging infrastructure (e.g., TensorBoard, WandB integration, or custom CSV logging)
- Existing benchmark scripts in `benchmarks/throughput_benchmark.py` or similar

### 1.3 Microbatch Configuration Discovery

Key code patterns to identify:
- How `num_microbatches` divides work: typically `gradient_accumulation_steps = num_microbatches`
- Relationship between microbatch size and global batch size:
  - If microbatch_size is fixed and num_microbatches varies → `global_batch = microbatch_size × num_microbatches × data_parallel_degree`
  - If global_batch is fixed and num_microbatches varies → `microbatch_size = global_batch / num_microbatches / data_parallel_degree`
- Look for comments or docstrings in scheduler implementations explaining this relationship

---

## 2. EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN

### 2.1 Core Hypothesis

**Primary Hypothesis**: 
- ZB-2p (two-pass ZeroBubble) maintains high throughput at low microbatch counts (M ≥ 2), outperforming 1F1B, 1F1B-I, and ZB-1p which require M ≥ 8-16 to reach peak throughput.

**Mechanistic Rationale for ZB-2p**:
- **1F1B** (naive): Sends forward pass downstream; blocks on backward pass. Bubbles occur when all pipeline stages don't have work. Requires large M to fill pipeline efficiently.
- **1F1B-I** (interleaved): Interleaves microbatches across pipeline stages to reduce bubbles, but still suffers from stragglers. Marginal improvement over 1F1B.
- **ZB-1p** (single-pass ZeroBubble): Uses dependency analysis to schedule forward and backward passes optimally but within a single iteration window. Still requires adequate M to keep all stages busy.
- **ZB-2p** (two-pass ZeroBubble): **KEY INSIGHT** – Fills bubbles by prefetching work from the next iteration. When stage i finishes its current iteration's backward pass, it immediately begins the next iteration's forward pass, maintaining continuous execution. This allows high utilization even at low M because the scheduler explicitly fills idle periods with future-iteration work. Trade-off: requires maintaining activations across iteration boundaries, increasing memory.

### 2.2 Experimental Parameters

**Independent Variable**: Number of microbatches (M)
- Values: {1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64}
- Rationale: Covers sparse (M=1-2, challenging regime), medium (M=4-16), and dense (M≥32, saturation regime)

**Fixed Parameters** (all methods held constant to isolate effect of M):

| Parameter | Value | Justification |
|-----------|-------|---|
| Model | Transformer-based LLM, ~7B parameters (or smaller for CPU testing) | Standard for pipeline parallelism studies; balanced compute per layer |
| Model architecture | 32-48 transformer layers | Creates 4-8 pipeline stages of 4-12 layers each |
| Task | Causal language modeling (forward + backward) | Matches ZB paper benchmarks; standard training setting |
| Microbatch size | 32 or 64 samples | **FIXED** – see discussion below |
| Data parallel degree | 1 (or 2 for multi-GPU baseline) | Isolates pipeline parallelism effects; no data parallelism confounds |
| Pipeline depth (P) | 4 stages (primary) | Minimum for meaningful pipeline study; each stage ≥1 GPU |
| Sequence length | 2048 tokens | Consistent with LLM standards |
| Optimizer | AdamW (fixed hyperparams across all methods) | Standard; prevents optimizer choice from affecting results |
| Learning rate | 1e-4 (or standard value for model size) | Fixed to ensure convergence equivalence |
| Number of iterations per trial | 100 (after 10 warmup iterations) | Sufficient for stable throughput averaging; warmup clears caches and initialization overhead |
| Number of independent trials | 3 | Captures variance across random seeds and system noise |

**Dependent Variables** (metrics collected per trial):

| Metric | Unit | Collection Method | Interpretation |
|--------|------|---|---|
| Throughput (primary) | samples/second | `total_samples / wall_clock_time` for iterations 11-100 | Higher is better; saturation indicates M* (optimal M) |
| Pipeline utilization | % | `(total_compute_time / (total_time × P)) × 100` | Indicates bubble percentage; 100% = no bubbles |
| Peak memory per stage | GB | Max allocated memory during iteration | Constraint on max feasible M |
| Iteration time | seconds/iteration | `wall_clock_time / num_iterations` | Lower is better; directly proportional to throughput |
| Gradient staleness | iterations | Max iterations backward pass lags forward pass | Proxy for convergence impact (secondary check) |

### 2.3 Batch Size Specification (Critical Clarification)

**Design Choice: Fix Microbatch Size, Vary Number of Microbatches**

This is the standard approach in ZeroBubble papers and ensures fair comparison:

```
Microbatch size (MB_SIZE) = FIXED at 32 or 64 samples
Number of microbatches (M) = VARIED {1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64}
Global batch size = MB_SIZE × M = {32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048}
Gradient accumulation steps = M
```

**Justification**:
1. **Isolates pipeline effects**: Varying M with fixed MB_SIZE tests whether scheduling methods efficiently utilize the accumulated gradients, not whether larger batches help training.
2. **Fair comparison**: All methods accumulate and apply gradients at the same logical points; differences are purely scheduling.
3. **Memory scaling**: As M increases, peak memory grows predictably (more in-flight activations), allowing us to identify memory-constrained maxima per method.
4. **Matches literature**: ZeroBubble paper uses exactly this parameterization (e.g., Figure 4-5).

**Alternative (Not Used)**:
- Fix global batch size and shrink microbatch size as M increases. This is less common and confounds the comparison: smaller microbatches reduce per-GPU compute, potentially masking scheduling benefits.

### 2.4 Measurement Protocol

**Setup Phase**:
1. Load pretrained model weights (or initialize with fixed seed for reproducibility)
2. Create synthetic dataset (DataLoader with fixed random seed, batch sampler set to deterministic mode)
3. Initialize optimizer and learning rate scheduler

**Per-Trial Execution** (for each method × M × trial_idx):
1. Initialize method-specific scheduler with `num_microbatches=M`, `pipeline_depth=P`
2. Run 10 warmup iterations (NOT included in throughput calculation)
   - Clears GPU caches, initializes cudnn algorithms
3. Reset timing and sample counter
4. Run 100 benchmark iterations:
   - Record `t_start` (wall clock), `samples_processed` at iteration start
   - Execute scheduler's forward-backward-step cycle
   - Record `t_end` at iteration completion
   - Collect memory and bubble metrics (if available via profiling hooks)
5. Post-trial:
   - Calculate throughput = `sum(samples_processed) / (t_end - t_start)`
   - Compute peak memory from profiling logs
   - Calculate utilization as `1 - (total_bubble_cycles / (P × total_cycles))`

**Logging**:
- All measurements saved to per-trial log: `results/method_{METHOD}_M_{M}_trial_{TRIAL}.csv`
- Columns: iteration, samples_in_iteration, iteration_time, peak_memory_mb, pipeline_util_%

### 2.5 Expected Outcomes & Hypotheses

**H1: 1F1B throughput improves with M**
- Prediction: Throughput ∝ M^(α) where α ∈ [0.3, 0.7] (sublinear, diminishing returns)
- Expected values (example, method-dependent):
  - M=1: 100 samples/sec (baseline, heavy bubbles)
  - M=4: 200-250 samples/sec
  - M=16: 350-400 samples/sec
  - M=64: 400-420 samples/sec (saturation)
- Saturation M* ≈ 16-32

**H2: 1F1B-I shows marginal improvement over 1F1B**
- Prediction: Throughput(1F1B-I, M) ≥ Throughput(1F1B, M) ∀ M, with typical gain +5-15%
- Saturation M* ≈ 12-24

**H3: ZB-1p > 1F1B-I for all M**
- Prediction: Throughput(ZB-1p, M) ≥ Throughput(1F1B-I, M) + 10% consistently
- Saturation M* ≈ 8-16

**H4: ZB-2p achieves high throughput at low M (MAIN RESULT)**
- Prediction: Throughput(ZB-2p, M=4) ≥ 0.90 × Throughput(ZB-2p, M=64)
- Prediction: Throughput(ZB-2p, M=4) > Throughput(ZB-1p, M=16)
- Saturation M* ≈ 2-4 (early plateau)
- Interpretation: ZB-2p's two-pass mechanism keeps pipeline full even with few microbatches

**H5: Method rankings may invert at high M**
- Prediction: At M ≥ 32, all methods converge to similar throughput (≈90-95% of ceiling)
- Interpretation: At high M, scheduling overhead diminishes; memory becomes bottleneck

### 2.6 Validation & Correctness Checks

1. **Loss curves equivalence**:
   - Plot training loss vs. iteration for each method at M=4
   - All curves must be within ±0.01% of each other (proof of algorithmic correctness)
   - If divergent: indicates method implementations differ fundamentally

2. **Monotonicity check**:
   - For each method, verify throughput(M) ≥ throughput(M/2) - 2% (accounting for noise)
   - If not: indicates measurement error or cache effects

3. **Saturation point identification**:
   - For each method, compute M* = min(M: throughput(M+2) < throughput(M) × 1.02)
   - Confirm M*(ZB-2p) < M*(ZB-1p) < M*(1F1B) (order validates hypothesis)

4. **Memory constraint validation**:
   - Track peak_memory(M) for each method
   - Confirm peak_memory is monotonically increasing (or at least non-decreasing)
   - Flag if peak_memory > 80GB on 80GB GPU: indicates method is memory-constrained, not compute-limited

5. **Ceiling throughput check**:
   - Compare max throughput across all methods to single-GPU baseline
   - Ratio should be: baseline_throughput / max_pipeline_throughput ≈ 1.0 to 1.5 (pipeline overhead expected)
   - If ratio > 2: indicates implementation inefficiency

### 2.7 Controls & Baselines

| Control | Purpose | Expected Outcome |
|---------|---------|---|
| **Single-GPU baseline** | Throughput ceiling (no pipeline) | Establishes max achievable throughput; pipeline methods should be within 80-120% (accounting for communication overhead) |
| **1F1B with M=1** | Worst-case pipeline scheduling | Lowest throughput; demonstrates need for M > 1 |
| **Synchronous data parallelism (if available)** | Alternative parallelism strategy | Sanity check; should have different memory/throughput tradeoff |
| **Identical random seeds across methods** | Eliminate initialization variance | Ensures comparisons are fair; variance comes only from scheduling |

### 2.8 Analysis & Visualization

**Primary Outputs**:
1. **Throughput curve plot** (4 lines, one per method):
   - X-axis: Number of microbatches (log scale, 1 to 64)
   - Y-axis: Throughput in samples/second
   - Error bars: ±1 std dev across 3 trials
   - Annotation: Saturation point (M*) for each method

2. **Relative performance table**:
   ```
   | Method | M=1 | M=2 | M=4 | M=8 | M=16 | M=32 | M=64 | M*(sat) |
   |--------|-----|-----|-----|-----|------|------|------|---------|
   | 1F1B   | 100% (baseline) | 130% | 180% | 250% | 330% | 380% | 400% | 16 |
   | 1F1B-I | 105% | 140% | 190% | 265% | 350% | 400% | 420% | 12 |
   | ZB-1p  | 115% | 160% | 220% | 300% | 380% | 420% | 450% | 8 |
   | ZB-2p  | 180% | 300% | 400% | 420% | 430% | 435% | 440% | 2 |
   ```
   (Values are illustrative; actual results depend on hardware/model)

3. **Pipeline utilization heatmap** (4 methods × 7 M values):
   - Color intensity: Bubble percentage (0-100%)
   - Darker (lower bubble) = better
   - Shows mechanism: ZB-2p maintains >85% utilization at M≥2

4. **Memory consumption plot**:
   - X-axis: M
   - Y-axis: Peak memory (GB) per stage
   - 4 lines (one per method)
   - Identifies memory-constrained regime

5. **Summary statistics table**:
   ```
   | Metric | 1F1B | 1F1B-I | ZB-1p | ZB-2p |
   |--------|------|--------|-------|-------|
   | Max throughput (M=64) | 400 | 420 | 450 | 440 |
   | Throughput@M=4 / Max | 45% | 45% | 49% | 91% |
   | Saturation M* | 16 | 12 | 8 | 2 |
   | Peak memory @ M=64 | 24GB | 25GB | 26GB | 32GB |
   ```

---

## 3. FEASIBILITY ANALYSIS

### 3.1 Hardware Requirements

**Minimum Configuration** (Primary Experiment):
- **GPUs**: 4 GPUs (for 4-stage pipeline) of:
  - NVIDIA A100 (40GB) or V100 (32GB) for 7B model
  - Or H100 (80GB) for larger models (13B+)
- **CPU cores**: 16-32 cores for data loading and preprocessing
- **Host memory (CPU RAM)**: 256GB+ (for dataset caching and model checkpoints)
- **Storage**: 200GB+ NVMe for model checkpoints, logs, and dataset

**Alternative: CPU-only testing** (for design validation only):
- Smaller model (~100M-1B params) can run on CPU
- Much slower (≈100-1000× slower), useful for correctness checks only
- Not recommended for final throughput measurements

**Scaling Options**:
- **8 GPUs**: Enables 8-stage pipeline; stronger test of methods
- **2 GPUs**: Single benchmark (M=1 and M=2 only) as sanity check; bottlenecked by limited parallelism

### 3.2 Estimated Wall-Clock Time

**Per single trial** (1 method, 1 M value, 3 trials):

```
Warmup iterations (10): ~30-60 seconds
Benchmark iterations (100): ~300-600 seconds
Data I/O overhead: ~30-60 seconds per trial
Total per trial: ~7-15 minutes (depending on hardware, model size)
```

**Full experiment matrix** (4 methods × 7 M values × 3 trials):

```
Single-trial time: ~10 minutes (average)
Total trials: 84
Sequential execution: 84 × 10 min = 840 minutes ≈ 14 hours

Parallel execution (if 4 GPUs running different trials):
  - Can run ~1 trial per 4-GPU setup at a time
  - Still ~14 hours sequentially across all methods/M
  - If HPC cluster available: can parallelize across multiple 4-GPU sets
  - Realistic turnaround: 2-4 hours on 4-node cluster (16 GPUs total)
```

**Breakdown by phase**:
| Phase | Time | Parallelizable? |
|-------|------|---|
| Data preparation | 30 min | Yes (once per trial batch) |
| 1F1B × 7M × 3 trials | 2.5 hours | Yes (can run separate M values in parallel) |
| 1F1B-I × 7M × 3 trials | 2.5 hours | Yes |
| ZB-1p × 7M × 3 trials | 2.5 hours | Yes |
| ZB-2p × 7M × 3 trials | 2.5 hours | Yes (but may contend for GPU memory) |
| Analysis & visualization | 30 min | Yes (single machine) |
| **Total (sequential)** | **~11 hours** | — |
| **Total (optimal parallel)** | **~3 hours** | (4 separate 4-GPU setups) |

### 3.3 Memory Considerations & Constraints

**Per-stage memory breakdown** (for 7B model with P=4, microbatch_size=32):

```
Model weights (per stage): ~1.5 GB (1/4 of 7B)
Optimizer state (per stage): ~3 GB (2× model size for AdamW)
Activations (forward pass): ~1-2 GB per microbatch
Gradients (backward pass): ~1.5 GB per microbatch
Pipeline buffer (micro-batch states): ~0.5-1 GB per M value
Total overhead (per stage, M=1): ~10-12 GB
```

**Peak memory sensitivity to M**:
```
M=1: ~12 GB per stage
M=4: ~16 GB per stage (4× more in-flight activations)
M=16: ~25 GB per stage
M=32: ~35-40 GB per stage (may exceed 40GB A100)
M=64: ~50+ GB per stage (requires 80GB GPU or OOM)
```

**Method-specific memory overhead**:
- **1F1B**: Baseline, minimal overhead
- **1F1B-I**: ~0-5% additional (interleaving metadata)
- **ZB-1p**: ~5-10% additional (scheduling state)
- **ZB-2p**: **+20-30% additional** (maintains activations across iteration boundary)
  - Stores forward-pass activations for next iteration
  - Requires careful memory management; may OOM at lower M than others

**Implication**: ZB-2p's memory cost is the main constraint. On 40GB GPUs:
- ZB-2p may max out at M=16-24, even if compute allows M=64
- This is acceptable; the hypothesis focuses on *low M*, not high M

**Memory mitigation strategies** (if needed):
- Use activation checkpointing (recompute activations vs. storing)
- Reduce model size to 1-3B params
- Use FP8 or FP16 for activations (requires careful handling)

### 3.4 Practical Constraints & Risk Mitigation

| Risk | Impact | Mitigation |
|------|--------|---|
| **ZB-2p implementation incomplete** | Cannot measure ZB-2p | Implement reference version (GPT-2 level model); fallback to simulator |
| **Memory OOM at high M** | Cannot measure saturation regime | Reduce M max to 32; focus on low M hypothesis |
| **Hardware heterogeneous (mixed GPU models)** | Unfair scheduling comparison | Ensure all stages use identical GPU models |
| **Method implementations have bugs** | Wrong conclusions | Validate loss curves match, gradients checksums identical |
| **High variance in throughput** | Noisy results | Increase trials to 5, warmup to 20 iterations |
| **Throughput dominated by I/O, not compute** | Measurements don't reflect scheduling | Use synthetic data (generated on-GPU) to isolate scheduling |

### 3.5 Cost Estimate (if using cloud resources)

Assuming cloud GPU rental (e.g., AWS EC2 with 8× A100 GPUs):
```
8 A100 GPUs × $4/hour × 4 hours (optimal parallel) = $128
+ Storage/networking: ~$20
Total: ~$150 for full experiment
```

Much cheaper if using HPC cluster with allocation-based pricing.

---

## 4. SUMMARY: EXPERIMENTAL WORKFLOW

### 4.1 End-to-End Protocol

```
PHASE 1: SETUP (1-2 hours)
  1. Clone/pull ZeroBubble repository
  2. Install dependencies (PyTorch, HuggingFace Transformers, etc.)
  3. Download or generate synthetic dataset
  4. Verify all 4 methods can be invoked: test on small M (1-2) quickly
  5. Create output directories: results/logs, results/plots

PHASE 2: BASELINE & SANITY CHECKS (1 hour)
  1. Run single-GPU baseline (no pipeline): record max throughput
  2. Run 1F1B with M=1 (worst case): confirm low throughput
  3. Run all 4 methods with M=2: verify loss curves match
  4. If any method crashes: debug, reduce batch size, add checkpoints

PHASE 3: MAIN EXPERIMENT (8-10 hours)
  For each method in [1F1B, 1F1B-I, ZB-1p, ZB-2p]:
    For each M in [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64]:
      For trial in [1, 2, 3]:
        1. Execute scheduler with method, M, trial
        2. Log throughput, memory, utilization
        3. If error: record and continue (don't block)
        4. If OOM: mark M as infeasible for method, skip
        5. Save trial results to CSV

PHASE 4: ANALYSIS (2-3 hours)
  1. Aggregate results across trials (mean, std)
  2. Identify saturation points (M*) per method
  3. Validate hypotheses: monotonicity, method ranking, loss equivalence
  4. Generate plots and summary tables
  5. Document findings and exceptions

PHASE 5: PRESENTATION (1 hour)
  1. Write results summary
  2. Produce main paper-quality figure (throughput curves)
  3. Appendix with detailed tables, logs, code configuration
```

### 4.2 Success Criteria

**Experiment is successful if**:
1. ✅ All 4 methods run without crashing for M ∈ [1, 2, 4, 8, 16]
2. ✅ Loss curves match (within ±0.01%) across methods at same M
3. ✅ Throughput curves are monotonically increasing (or flat) with M ± 2% noise
4. ✅ ZB-2p saturation M* ≤ 4, other methods M* ≥ 8
5. ✅ ZB-2p(M=4) ≥ 0.85 × max_throughput, while 1F1B(M=4) ≤ 0.50 × max_throughput
6. ✅ Peak memory scales predictably; ZB-2p ≤ 50% higher than 1F1B at same M

**Partial success** (if any criteria fail):
- Likely cause: Implementation differences, hardware heterogeneity, or experimental parameters
- Action: Investigate, adjust parameters, rerun focused subset

---

## 5. ASSUMPTIONS & FIXED REQUIREMENTS

### Fixed Task Requirements (Non-negotiable)
1. Four scheduling methods must be under test: 1F1B, 1F1B-I, ZB-1p, ZB-2p
2. Primary metric is throughput (samples/second)
3. Question focuses on microbatch count as independent variable
4. Hypothesis: ZB-2p shows fundamentally different (better) behavior at low M

### Assumptions (Stated for Clarity)
1. **All methods are correctly implemented** and converge to identical loss
2. **Synchronous pipeline** (no asynchronous updates) across all methods
3. **Transformer model** with balanced layers per stage
4. **Microbatch size is fixed**, number of microbatches is varied (standard approach)
5. **4-8 GPU pipeline** is available; results may not extrapolate to >16 stages
6. **Throughput is compute-limited** at low M (not I/O or communication bottlenecked)
7. **No data augmentation or other stochasticity** affects loss convergence
8. **PyTorch or TensorFlow** backend; CUDA-capable GPUs available

---

## 6. UNCERTAINTIES & SENSITIVITY ANALYSIS

### Consequential Uncertainties

1. **Throughput metric definition**:
   - **Uncertainty**: Should "throughput" include communication time (AllReduce), gradient checkpointing overhead, or only pure forward/backward compute?
   - **Impact**: Different choices can change measured throughput by ±10-20%
   - **Resolution**: Pre-specify in code; use wall-clock time for entire iteration as denominator (includes all overheads)

2. **Memory bottleneck at high M**:
   - **Uncertainty**: Will ZB-2p hit OOM before reaching M=64?
   - **Impact**: May truncate saturation curve; unable to confirm convergence
   - **Resolution**: Measure peak memory; if approaching GPU limit, reduce max M or model size

3. **Pipeline depth generalization**:
   - **Uncertainty**: Do results (especially M*) change significantly if P is 4 vs 8 vs 16?
   - **Impact**: Conclusions may be depth-specific
   - **Resolution**: Run subset with P=8 as sensitivity analysis; note depth dependency in results

4. **Hardware heterogeneity**:
   - **Uncertainty**: If pipeline stages run on different GPU types (A100 vs V100), does scheduling still rank the same?
   - **Impact**: Method rankings may flip due to synchronization at slow stages
   - **Resolution**: Ensure all stages use identical GPU type; document hardware spec clearly

5. **Gradient staleness and convergence**:
   - **Uncertainty**: Do ZB methods' higher staleness (if any) slow convergence to target loss?
   - **Impact**: ZB-2p may achieve higher throughput but lower effective training efficiency (samples to convergence)
   - **Resolution**: Track convergence (iterations to loss threshold) as secondary metric; focus main analysis on fixed-iteration throughput

6. **Optimal M determination**:
   - **Uncertainty**: Is saturation point M* a sharp phase transition or gradual plateau?
   - **Impact**: May be hard to define M* precisely
   - **Resolution**: Define M* operationally as first M where throughput(M+2)/throughput(M) < 1.02 (≤2% improvement)

### Sensitivity Analysis Plan

If time permits, explore:
1. **Varying pipeline depth**: Repeat 1-2 methods with P=8 (vs. primary P=4)
2. **Varying model size**: Smaller (1B) and larger (13B) models as bounds
3. **Varying batch sizes**: Microbatch size = {16, 32, 64} to test scaling
4. **Varying number of iterations**: N ∈ {50, 100, 200} to confirm convergence of throughput estimates

---

## 7. CODE CONFIGURATION REFERENCE

### Example invocation (pseudo-code):

```bash
# Setup
git clone <zero-bubble-repo>
cd zero_bubble
pip install -r requirements.txt

# Baseline: single-GPU
python train.py \
  --model-size 7B \
  --num-iterations 100 \
  --warmup-iterations 10 \
  --log-throughput \
  --output-dir results/baseline

# 1F1B with M=4
python train.py \
  --schedule-method 1f1b \
  --num-microbatches 4 \
  --microbatch-size 32 \
  --num-stages 4 \
  --num-iterations 100 \
  --warmup-iterations 10 \
  --log-throughput \
  --log-bubbles \
  --log-memory \
  --output-dir results/1f1b_M4

# ZB-2p with M=4
python train.py \
  --schedule-method zb_2pass \
  --num-microbatches 4 \
  --microbatch-size 32 \
  --num-stages 4 \
  --num-iterations 100 \
  --warmup-iterations 10 \
  --log-throughput \
  --log-bubbles \
  --log-memory \
  --output-dir results/zb2p_M4
```

### Expected output (per trial):
```
results/zb2p_M4/trial_1/
  ├── log.txt
  ├── throughput.csv        # columns: iteration, samples, time_s, throughput_samples_sec
  ├── memory.csv            # columns: iteration, peak_memory_mb_per_stage
  ├── bubbles.csv           # columns: stage, bubble_percent
  └── loss.csv              # columns: iteration, loss
```

---

## 8. FINAL CHECKLIST

Before executing the experiment, verify:

- [ ] All 4 methods are present in codebase and runnable
- [ ] Microbatch count parameterization is accessible (CLI or config)
- [ ] Throughput logging exists or can be added easily
- [ ] Loss curves can be extracted and compared
- [ ] Memory profiling available (nvidia-smi or PyTorch profiler)
- [ ] 4+ GPUs available and uniform
- [ ] Warmup and benchmark iteration separation is implemented
- [ ] Random seeds fixed for reproducibility
- [ ] Data loader uses deterministic sampler
- [ ] Ground truth (expected behavior) aligned with ZeroBubble papers

---

## 9. CONCLUSION

This design proposes a rigorous, controlled experiment to test whether ZB-2p's two-pass scheduling mechanism delivers superior throughput efficiency at low microbatch counts compared to 1F1B, 1F1B-I, and ZB-1p. By fixing model, hardware, and optimizer while varying only the number of microbatches, we isolate the scheduling algorithm's effect. The expected result—that ZB-2p saturates throughput at M≈2-4 while others require M≥8-16—would validate the core innovation of ZeroBubble and help practitioners choose scheduling strategies for their workloads.

## Experiment Design Plan: Throughput Analysis of Pipeline Parallelism Scheduling Methods

### Key Research Question
Does the throughput for methods 1F1B, 1F1B-I, and ZB-1p improve as the number of microbatches increases, while ZB-2p maintains high throughput even with fewer microbatches?

### Proposed Experimental Approach

#### 1. **Independent Variables (Factors)**
- **Scheduling Method**: Four levels
  - 1F1B (One-Forward-One-Backward): Traditional baseline
  - 1F1B-I (1F1B with interleaving): Enhanced with pipeline interleaving
  - ZB-1p (Zero-Bubble single pipeline): Optimized for single-pass bubble reduction
  - ZB-2p (Zero-Bubble dual pipeline): Optimized for dual-pipeline efficiency
  
- **Number of Microbatches (M)**: 8-12 discrete levels
  - Proposed values: {2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 96, 128}
  - Rationale: Cover range from pipeline stages (typically 4-8) to high parallelism regime

#### 2. **Dependent Variable**
- **Throughput (primary metric)**: 
  - Samples per second (SPS) or iterations per second
  - Calculated as: (batch_size × num_microbatches) / total_training_time
  - Normalize to throughput relative to 1F1B baseline at M=2 for comparison

#### 3. **Control Variables (fixed across all trials)**
- Model architecture: GPT-like transformer (fixed depth and width)
- Pipeline stages: 4 or 8 stages (recommend 4 for clarity)
- Batch size per microbatch: Fixed (e.g., 32 or 64)
- Learning rate and optimizer settings
- Hardware configuration: Same GPU/CPU setup
- Training duration: Fixed number of iterations (e.g., 1000 steps to ensure statistical stability)

#### 4. **Experiment Matrix Design**

```
        M=2   M=4   M=6   M=8   M=12  M=16  M=24  M=32  M=48  M=64  M=96  M=128
1F1B     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓
1F1B-I   ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓
ZB-1p    ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓
ZB-2p    ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓
```
**Total configurations: 4 methods × 12 microbatch levels = 48 runs**

#### 5. **Throughput Measurement Approach**

- **Per-run measurement**:
  1. Warmup phase: First 50 iterations (excluded from measurement)
  2. Measurement phase: Next 500-1000 iterations
  3. Record: Total time, samples processed, memory usage
  
- **Calculation formula**:
  ```
  Throughput = (num_iterations × batch_size_per_microbatch × M) / measurement_time_seconds
  ```

- **Normalization**:
  ```
  Normalized_Throughput = Throughput_method / Throughput_1F1B_M=2
  ```

#### 6. **Statistical Design**
- **Replicates**: 3 runs per configuration (account for variance)
- **Key metrics per configuration**:
  - Mean throughput
  - Standard deviation
  - Min/max values
  - Memory peak usage (indicator of efficiency)

#### 7. **Expected Outcomes & Interpretation Criteria**

| Method | Expected Pattern | Interpretation |
|--------|------------------|-----------------|
| 1F1B | Linear/sublinear growth with M | Baseline: throughput gains plateau as M increases due to pipeline bubbles |
| 1F1B-I | Improved growth compared to 1F1B | Interleaving reduces bubble overhead, better scaling |
| ZB-1p | Near-linear growth until saturation | Zero-bubble strategy maintains growth, peaks at moderate-high M |
| ZB-2p | **Flat/high throughput across M range** | Key distinguisher: maintains efficiency with fewer microbatches |

#### 8. **Key Assertions to Validate**
- **Hypothesis H1**: ZB-2p throughput at M=2 ≥ 1F1B throughput at M=32
- **Hypothesis H2**: 1F1B, 1F1B-I, ZB-1p show improved throughput as M increases (positive slope in log-linear plot)
- **Hypothesis H3**: ZB-2p throughput improvement slope << other methods (nearly constant across M range)

#### 9. **Critical Assumptions**
- Four scheduling methods are fully implemented and correct in the target codebase
- Pipeline depth is known and can be set to a standard value (e.g., 4 or 8)
- Microbatch count is the only scheduling parameter varied (other pipeline parameters held constant)
- Training is deterministic or variance is low (for reproducibility)
- Measurements are wall-clock time (not simulated/theoretical estimates)

#### 10. **Uncertainties & Potential Confounds**
- **Memory pressure**: Higher M may cause OOM or cache effects not captured in throughput
- **Hardware saturation**: May not see clear differences if hardware is underutilized
- **Warmup effects**: Initial iterations may not be representative
- **Method implementation quality**: Buggy implementation could mask algorithmic differences
- **Model size sensitivity**: Results may vary significantly with model depth/width
- **Synchronization overhead**: Communication costs between stages may dominate at certain scales

#### 11. **Feasibility Checks (Before Full Experiment)**
1. Verify all four methods compile and initialize without error
2. Conduct a pilot run: 1F1B with M=4 and M=16 to confirm throughput varies with M
3. Estimate total compute time: 48 configs × 3 replicates × ~10 min per run ≈ 24 GPU-hours
4. Check memory ceiling: Verify no OOM at M=128 with selected model size

#### 12. **Data Collection & Analysis Plan**
- **Output format**: CSV with columns [method, num_microbatches, run_id, throughput_sps, memory_peak_mb, wall_clock_time_sec]
- **Visualization**: 
  - Line plot: Throughput vs. M (separate lines per method) → confirms hypothesis patterns
  - Box plot: Throughput distribution per method → shows variance
  - Heatmap: Throughput matrix [method × M] → easy identification of sweet spots
- **Statistical test**: Two-way ANOVA to assess significance of method and M effects

#### 13. **Success Criteria**
The experiment design will be considered successful if:
1. All 48 configurations complete without error
2. Clear differentiation in throughput curves by scheduling method is visible
3. ZB-2p shows distinctly different growth pattern (flatter) vs. other three methods
4. Results are reproducible across replicates (CV < 5% for most runs)
5. Data supports or refutes H1, H2, H3 hypotheses with statistical confidence (p < 0.05)

## Final Experiment Design: Throughput Analysis of Pipeline Parallelism Scheduling Methods

### Research Question
Does the throughput for methods 1F1B, 1F1B-I, and ZB-1p improve as the number of microbatches increases, while ZB-2p maintains high throughput even with fewer microbatches?

---

## 1. EXPERIMENTAL FRAMEWORK

### 1.1 Independent Variables (Factors)

#### Factor 1: Scheduling Method (4 levels)
- **1F1B** (One-Forward-One-Backward): Traditional baseline with stage-wise scheduling
- **1F1B-I** (1F1B with interleaving): Enhanced variant with pipeline interleaving optimization
- **ZB-1p** (Zero-Bubble single pipeline): Single pipeline with explicit bubble reduction
- **ZB-2p** (Zero-Bubble dual pipeline): Dual pipeline strategy optimized for reduced-microbatch regime

#### Factor 2: Number of Microbatches (M) - 12 levels
**REVISED with stage-count consideration:**
- **If pipeline stages p=4**: M ∈ {4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 96, 128, 192}
- **If pipeline stages p=8**: M ∈ {8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 96, 128, 192, 256, 384}

**Rationale for M ≥ p constraint:**
- Standard pipeline scheduling requires at minimum p microbatches to saturate the pipeline (one sample per stage during warmup)
- Using M < p would result in incomplete utilization and cannot properly test the scheduling methods' ability to reduce bubbles
- Typically, effective bubble reduction becomes observable when M ≥ 2p (dual-pipeline saturation)

**Relative ratio interpretation for ZB-2p:**
- "Low M" is defined as M ∈ [p, 2p) where traditional methods still exhibit significant bubbles
- "High M" is defined as M ≥ 2p where most methods approach saturated throughput
- **Key hypothesis**: ZB-2p maintains >90% of peak throughput even at M=p, while 1F1B/1F1B-I may only achieve ~60-70%

#### Factor 3: Pipeline Depth (p) - 2 levels (NEW)
- **p = 4 stages**: Shallow pipeline (typical for testing, faster computation)
- **p = 8 stages**: Deeper pipeline (more realistic for large models, higher bubble ratio potential)

**Rationale:**
- Bubble severity scales with p/M ratio; comparing p=4 and p=8 directly tests ZB-2p's robustness across pipeline depths
- Expected behavior: ZB-2p advantage should be more pronounced at p=8 (higher baseline bubble ratio with 1F1B)
- Allows assessment of whether method effectiveness is depth-dependent

### 1.2 Dependent Variable (Primary)

**Throughput (samples per second, SPS):**
$$\text{Throughput} = \frac{\text{batch\_size\_per\_microbatch} \times \text{M} \times \text{iterations\_in\_measurement}}{\text{wall\_clock\_time\_seconds}}$$

**Calculation details:**
- Window: Exclude first 50 iterations (warmup), measure next 500-1000 iterations
- Unit: Samples/second or iterations/second (with explicit conversion factor documented)
- Record: Raw throughput and timing components (forward time, backward time, communication time if traceable)

### 1.3 Dependent Variables (Secondary)

- **Memory peak usage** (MB): Peak GPU memory during measurement window
- **Bubble ratio estimate**: (Theoretical peak time - actual time) / Theoretical peak time
- **Iteration variance** (std dev of per-iteration times): Indicator of scheduling stability

---

## 2. EXPERIMENT MATRIX

### 2.1 Full Factorial Design: 4 methods × 12 M values × 2 pipeline depths = **96 configurations**

```
MATRIX FOR p=4:
        M=4   M=6   M=8   M=12  M=16  M=24  M=32  M=48  M=64  M=96  M=128 M=192
1F1B     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓
1F1B-I   ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓
ZB-1p    ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓
ZB-2p    ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓

MATRIX FOR p=8:
        M=8   M=12  M=16  M=24  M=32  M=48  M=64  M=96  M=128 M=192 M=256 M=384
1F1B     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓
1F1B-I   ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓
ZB-1p    ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓
ZB-2p    ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓     ✓
```

**Total experimental runs:** 96 configurations × 3 replicates = **288 runs**

### 2.2 Factorial Design Justification
- **Methods** factor: Tests the core hypothesis about algorithmic differences
- **Microbatches** factor: Tests whether throughput scales with M; **crucial for distinguishing methods**
- **Pipeline depth** factor: Tests robustness of ZB-2p across architectural scales; identifies depth-dependent effects

---

## 3. CONTROL VARIABLES (Fixed Across All Runs)

### 3.1 Model Architecture
- **Model type**: GPT-style transformer (or comparable model with configurable depth)
- **Hidden dimension**: Fixed at 768 (or appropriate for GPU memory limit)
- **Number of layers**: Equal to pipeline depth p (e.g., 4 or 8 layers, partitioned into p stages)
- **Attention heads**: Fixed (e.g., 12)
- **Sequence length**: Fixed (e.g., 1024 tokens)

### 3.2 Batch and Data Configuration
- **Global batch size**: batch_size_per_microbatch × M (e.g., 32 × M)
- **Batch size per microbatch**: Fixed at 32 (or 64 if memory permits)
- **Data parallelism degree**: **1 (isolated to test pipeline parallelism only)**
- **Dataset**: Synthetic data (deterministic, no I/O variance) or cached real data

### 3.3 Training Configuration
- **Learning rate**: Fixed (e.g., 0.001)
- **Optimizer**: Fixed (e.g., Adam with β1=0.9, β2=0.999)
- **Gradient accumulation**: Disabled (direct microbatch processing)
- **Gradient checkpointing**: Fixed across all runs (either all enabled or all disabled); **document clearly**
  - If enabled: Applies uniformly to all methods for fair memory comparison
  - If disabled: More direct throughput comparison without checkpointing overhead

### 3.4 Pipeline Configuration
- **Stage partition**: Explicit assignment of transformer layers to stages (e.g., layers 1-2 to stage 1, etc.)
- **Activation checkpointing strategy**: Same across methods (checkpoint every N layers if applicable)
- **Communication backend**: NCCL (or equivalent GPU-optimized backend)
  - NCCL version: Fixed
  - Buffer size**: Fixed (e.g., 128 MB)
  - All-reduce algorithm: Fixed (e.g., ring or tree, whichever is default)

### 3.5 Execution Environment
- **Hardware**: Fixed GPU model(s), same setup across all runs
- **CUDA version**: Fixed
- **cuDNN version**: Fixed
- **CPU affinity**: If applicable, fix to same core set
- **Process synchronization**: Use barriers/events to ensure deterministic ordering

### 3.6 Measurement Parameters
- **Warmup iterations**: 50 (to allow JIT compilation, kernel optimization)
- **Measurement window**: 500-1000 iterations (or duration: ≥30 seconds for stability)
- **Synchronization**: Explicit GPU synchronization before/after timing windows to avoid asynchrony artifacts

---

## 4. THROUGHPUT MEASUREMENT & NORMALIZATION

### 4.1 Raw Throughput Measurement
**Primary metric (absolute):**
$$\text{Throughput}_{\text{raw}} = \frac{M \times \text{batch\_size} \times \text{measured\_iterations}}{\text{wall\_clock\_time\_sec}}$$

**Calculation details:**
- Window: Exclude first 50 iterations (warmup), measure next 500-1000 iterations
- Record: Raw throughput and timing components (forward time, backward time, communication time if traceable)

### 4.2 Normalization Schemes (Multiple for Robustness)

#### Scheme A: Peak-Normalized Throughput
$$\text{Throughput}_{\text{normalized\_A}} = \frac{\text{Throughput}_{\text{method, p, M}}}{\max(\text{Throughput}_{\text{all methods, p, M=high}})}$$
- Denominator: Maximum observed throughput for each pipeline depth (typically at highest M)
- Range: [0, 1], easier to compare methods within same pipeline depth
- **Issue**: If M=2 not runnable, use M=p or M=2p as baseline

#### Scheme B: Theoretical Peak Normalized
$$\text{Bubble\_ratio} = 1 - \frac{\text{Throughput}_{\text{actual}}}{\text{Throughput}_{\text{theoretical\_peak}}}$$

Where:
$$\text{Throughput}_{\text{theoretical\_peak}} = \frac{\text{GPU\_compute\_capacity (FLOPs/sec)}}{\text{FLOPs\_per\_sample}} = \text{samples\_per\_second\_without\_bubbles}$$

**Calculation:**
- Measure theoretical peak by running a single forward-backward pass with all stages active (no pipelining)
- Serves as bubble-rate indicator (0 = no bubbles, 1 = complete idle)
- **Advantage**: Makes bubble reduction directly visible across methods

#### Scheme C: 1F1B-Relative Baseline
$$\text{Speedup} = \frac{\text{Throughput}_{\text{method, p, M}}}{\text{Throughput}_{\text{1F1B, p, M}}}$$
- Denominator: 1F1B throughput at same (p, M) configuration
- Shows method superiority/inferiority relative to traditional baseline
- **Only apply for M ≥ p to ensure 1F1B is runnable**

### 4.3 Recommended Normalization for Final Report
- **Report all three schemes** to provide multiple perspectives
- Primary analysis: Scheme B (bubble ratio) to directly assess zero-bubble hypothesis
- Secondary analysis: Scheme C (speedup) for practical impact assessment
- Absolute throughput reported alongside all normalized values for transparency

---

## 5. STATISTICAL ANALYSIS PLAN

### 5.1 Descriptive Statistics (Per Configuration)
- Mean throughput (μ)
- Standard deviation (σ)
- Coefficient of variation (CV = σ/μ), target CV < 5% per configuration
- Min/max across replicates
- 95% confidence interval on mean

### 5.2 Two-Way ANOVA (Primary Test)

**Factors:** Method (4 levels) × Microbatches (12 levels), **separately for each pipeline depth p**

**Model:**
$$\text{Throughput}_{i,j,k} = \mu + \text{Method}_i + \text{Microbatch}_j + (\text{Method} \times \text{Microbatch})_{ij} + \epsilon_{i,j,k}$$

where k indexes replicates.

**Hypotheses tested:**
- **H0_method**: All methods have equal mean throughput → Rejected if p < 0.05 → Supports method differentiation
- **H0_M**: All microbatch counts have equal mean throughput → Rejected if p < 0.05 → Supports M scaling effect
- **H0_interaction**: No method × M interaction → Rejected if p < 0.05 → Confirms methods scale differently with M

### 5.3 Trend Analysis: Linear Regression of Throughput vs. M

**For each method and pipeline depth**, fit:
$$\text{Throughput} = \alpha + \beta \cdot \log_2(M) + \epsilon$$

or equivalently:

$$\text{Throughput} = \alpha + \beta \cdot M + \epsilon$$

(choice between log/linear based on preliminary data visualization)

**Extract slope coefficient β for each method:**

| Method | p=4 slope | p=8 slope | Interpretation |
|--------|-----------|-----------|-----------------|
| 1F1B | β₁,₄ | β₁,₈ | Expected: positive, moderate magnitude |
| 1F1B-I | β₂,₄ | β₂,₈ | Expected: positive, magnitude < 1F1B |
| ZB-1p | β₃,₄ | β₃,₈ | Expected: positive, but smaller than 1F1B |
| ZB-2p | β₄,₄ | β₄,₈ | Expected: near zero (flat curve) |

**Statistical tests on slopes:**

1. **Test H2**: Slope significantly positive (one-tailed t-test)
   - H0: β₁ ≤ 0, H1: β₁ > 0 for 1F1B, 1F1B-I, ZB-1p
   - Target: Reject H0 with p < 0.05

2. **Test H3 (key test)**: ZB-2p slope not significantly different from zero (two-tailed t-test)
   - H0: β₄ = 0, H1: β₄ ≠ 0
   - Target: Fail to reject H0 (p > 0.05) indicates flat throughput curve

3. **Slope comparison**: ZB-2p slope << other methods (pairwise contrast)
   - H0: β₄ - β_i ≥ -ε (where ε is small margin), H1: β₄ - β_i < -ε
   - Test whether |β₄| < 0.1 × mean(|β₁, β₂, β₃|) (i.e., ZB-2p slope is <10% of others)

### 5.4 Three-Way ANOVA (Pipeline Depth Sensitivity)

**Optional extended model including pipeline depth:**
$$\text{Throughput}_{i,j,l,k} = \mu + \text{Method}_i + \text{Microbatch}_j + \text{Depth}_l + (\text{Method} \times \text{Depth})_{il} + \cdots + \epsilon$$

**Purpose:** Identify whether method effectiveness varies significantly with pipeline depth (robustness test)
**Expected result for ZB-2p:** Method × Depth interaction should be minimal (ZB-2p consistently strong at both p=4 and p=8)

---

## 6. EXPECTED OUTCOMES & VALIDATION CRITERIA

### 6.1 Hypothesized Throughput Patterns

#### For p=4 (shallow pipeline):

| Method | M=4 (low) | M=12 (mid) | M=32 (high) | Pattern | Rationale |
|--------|-----------|-----------|-----------|---------|-----------|
| **1F1B** | 60-70% peak | 75-85% peak | 85-92% peak | ↗ Upward curve | Incomplete saturation, bubbles decrease with M |
| **1F1B-I** | 70-80% peak | 82-90% peak | 90-95% peak | ↗ Upward curve, higher than 1F1B | Interleaving reduces bubble overhead |
| **ZB-1p** | 75-85% peak | 88-94% peak | 95-98% peak | ↗ Steep rise, then plateau | Zero-bubble algorithm, reaches saturation faster |
| **ZB-2p** | **88-95% peak** | **93-97% peak** | **95-98% peak** | ≈ Flat high curve | Dual-pipeline design: high efficiency at low M |

#### For p=8 (deep pipeline):

| Method | M=8 (low) | M=24 (mid) | M=64 (high) | Pattern | Rationale |
|--------|-----------|-----------|-----------|---------|-----------|
| **1F1B** | 45-55% peak | 65-75% peak | 80-88% peak | ↗ Shallow rise | High baseline bubbles (p/M=1 initially), slow saturation |
| **1F1B-I** | 55-70% peak | 75-85% peak | 88-93% peak | ↗ Steeper rise | Interleaving helps, but still method-limited |
| **ZB-1p** | 70-80% peak | 85-92% peak | 93-97% peak | ↗ Steep rise, plateaus | Better bubble elimination, reaches saturation at moderate M |
| **ZB-2p** | **82-92% peak** | **92-96% peak** | **96-98% peak** | ≈ Flat high curve | Robust across M range; dual-pipeline advantage more pronounced |

**Key visual signature:** When plotting throughput vs. M on semi-log or linear scale:
- 1F1B, 1F1B-I, ZB-1p: Curves showing clear increase then plateau
- ZB-2p: Relatively flat line near top of plot from low M onwards

### 6.2 Quantitative Validation Criteria

#### Criterion 1: ZB-2p Throughput at Low M
$$\text{Throughput}_{\text{ZB-2p, p, M=p}} \geq 0.85 \times \text{Throughput}_{\text{ZB-2p, p, M=\text{high}}}$$

**Interpretation:** ZB-2p maintains ≥85% of peak throughput even when M=p (minimum recommended)
**Acceptance threshold:** Both p=4 and p=8 satisfy this

#### Criterion 2: Relative Improvement of ZB-2p over 1F1B at M=p
$$\text{Speedup}_{\text{ZB-2p vs 1F1B}} = \frac{\text{Throughput}_{\text{ZB-2p, p, M=p}}}{\text{Throughput}_{\text{1F1B, p, M=p}}} \geq 1.3$$

**Interpretation:** ZB-2p is ≥30% faster than 1F1B at the minimum microbatch count
**Rationale:** At low M, 1F1B suffers from high bubble ratio, ZB-2p should excel
**Acceptance threshold:** Both p=4 and p=8 show ≥1.3× speedup

#### Criterion 3: Slope Difference (H3 validation)
$$|\text{slope}_{\text{ZB-2p}}| < 0.1 \times \text{mean}(|\text{slope}_{\text{1F1B}}, |\text{slope}_{\text{1F1B-I}}|, |\text{slope}_{\text{ZB-1p}}|)$$

**Interpretation:** ZB-2p slope (in throughput vs. M) is <10% of average slope of other three methods
**Statistical test:** One-sided test of slope difference, p < 0.05
**Acceptance threshold:** p=4 and p=8 both satisfy criterion independently

#### Criterion 4: Throughput Stability (Coefficient of Variation)
$$\text{CV}_{\text{method, p, M}} = \frac{\sigma}{\mu} < 0.05 \quad \text{for} \quad \geq 90\% \text{ of configurations}$$

**Interpretation:** Variance within replicates is low, confirming stable measurement
**Acceptance threshold:** Only <10% of 96 configs exceed CV=5%

#### Criterion 5: No Significant Method × Depth Interaction for ZB-2p
$$\text{Interaction effect}_{(\text{ZB-2p} \times \text{Depth})} \text{ not significant (p > 0.10)}$$

**Interpretation:** ZB-2p's advantage persists consistently across pipeline depths (robustness)
**Statistical test:** Three-way ANOVA interaction term

---

## 7. PRELIMINARY ASSUMPTIONS

### 7.1 Technical Assumptions
1. All four scheduling methods (1F1B, 1F1B-I, ZB-1p, ZB-2p) are **correctly implemented** and functionally correct in the target codebase
2. Methods are **properly configurable** with explicit microbatch count parameter (no hardcoded defaults)
3. Pipeline **stage partitioning is flexible** and can be set to both p=4 and p=8 without architectural conflicts
4. **Data parallelism is disabled** (degree = 1) to isolate pipeline parallelism effects
5. **Gradient checkpointing strategy is consistent** across all methods (either all enabled or all disabled uniformly)
6. **Deterministic execution** is achievable, or variance is low enough for statistical differentiation (target: inter-replicate CV < 5%)
7. **Memory capacity** is sufficient to run M=192 at p=4 or M=384 at p=8 without OOM (may require smaller batch sizes if needed)
8. **NCCL communication** backend is stable and has deterministic performance across runs

### 7.2 Methodological Assumptions
1. **Wall-clock time measurement** accurately reflects scheduling overhead (not simulated/theoretical estimates)
2. **Warmup of 50 iterations** is sufficient for kernel fusion and optimization to stabilize
3. **Measurement window of 500-1000 iterations** is long enough to amortize synchronization overhead
4. **No external system interference** during measurement phase (fixed CPU clock, no background processes)
5. **Synthetic or cached data** eliminates I/O as a confounding variable
6. **Per-method overhead** (parameter initialization, graph compilation) is the same across methods or negligible relative to throughput differences

### 7.3 Algorithmic Assumptions
1. **1F1B** baseline can indeed only achieve ~60-70% efficiency at M=p with p=8 (standard literature finding)
2. **Zero-bubble strategies** (ZB-1p, ZB-2p) are theoretically designed to reduce bubbles; implementation follows theory
3. **ZB-2p's dual-pipeline design** fundamentally differs from single-pipeline variants, justifying flat throughput curve hypothesis
4. **Bubble ratio scales primarily with p/M ratio**, not other hardware-specific factors

---

## 8. UNCERTAINTIES & POTENTIAL CONFOUNDS

### 8.1 Known Uncertainties
1. **Optimal microbatch range:** May differ from proposed 2-3× and 4-24× pipeline depth; adaptive sampling (e.g., binary search for saturation M) may be needed
2. **Memory-induced bottlenecks:** Higher M may trigger:
   - OOM requiring batch size reduction (confounds throughput metric)
   - Cache misses or page swaps (non-linear performance degradation)
   - Gradient accumulation complexity (if enabled)

3. **Variance magnitude:** System jitter, CUDA kernel scheduling, NCCL synchronization may cause CV > 5% in some configurations; unknown without pilot runs

4. **Implementation robustness:** 
   - ZB-2p may have subtle bugs or suboptimal implementation reducing its theoretical advantage
   - Different optimization levels for different methods in same codebase

5. **Saturation point uncertainty:** Each method may saturate at different M values; precise saturation point unknown a priori

6. **GPU saturation vs. communication bottleneck:** Unclear whether throughput is limited by compute (methods' scheduling efficiency) or by communication (network bandwidth)

### 8.2 Potential Confounds

| Confound | Mitigation |
|----------|-----------|
| **Kernel optimization variability** | Use same CUDA version, same GPU model, warmup phase with repeated runs |
| **Different compilation artifacts** | Build all methods in single binary if possible; use same compiler flags |
| **NCCL ring/tree algorithm selection** | Explicitly set NCCL_ALGO environment variable to fixed value |
| **Host-device synchronization latency** | Time only device-side operations (CUDA events) separately; ensure consistent sync points |
| **GPU clock throttling** | Fix GPU frequency if possible; monitor during runs; exclude outliers if thermal throttling detected |
| **Data layout and cache effects** | Use identical tensor allocation and layout across methods; no method-specific optimizations |
| **Floating-point determinism** | Set environment flags for deterministic CUDA operations (cuDNN determinism flag, etc.) |
| **Different backward pass implementations** | Verify all methods use identical backward graph structure; only forward scheduling differs |

### 8.3 Sensitivity Analysis Recommendations
- **If significant variance detected:** Increase replicates from 3 to 5 for high-variance configurations
- **If saturation point differs significantly:** Add extra M values near saturation points to characterize curves precisely
- **If memory becomes limiting:** Reduce global batch size proportionally and document scaling adjustment
- **If GPU saturation reached before expected M:** Add additional hardware factors (e.g., GPU memory bandwidth utilization) to analysis

---

## 9. FEASIBILITY CHECKLIST (Pre-Experiment)

Before committing to full 288-run experiment:

### 9.1 Code Verification Phase
- [ ] Verify all four methods compile without error
- [ ] Confirm microbatch parameter is exposed and configurable (not hardcoded)
- [ ] Verify pipeline depth is configurable independently to 4 and 8
- [ ] Check that data parallelism can be set to degree=1
- [ ] Confirm gradient checkpointing status is consistent across methods

### 9.2 Pilot Experiment Phase (Estimate: 1-2 GPU-hours)
**Run minimal representative subset:**
- **Configuration 1:** 1F1B, p=4, M=4, 1 replicate → verify execution
- **Configuration 2:** 1F1B, p=4, M=32, 1 replicate → verify throughput is higher
- **Configuration 3:** ZB-2p, p=4, M=4, 1 replicate → verify throughput is competitive
- **Configuration 4:** ZB-2p, p=4, M=32, 1 replicate → verify throughput saturation

**Pilot success criteria:**
- All four configurations complete without crashes
- Throughput difference between M=4 and M=32 is visible (>10% difference)
- Absolute throughput values are reasonable (not suspiciously high or low)
- Replicate variance estimates allow estimation of true sample size needed

### 9.3 Resource Planning
**Estimated compute budget:**
- 48 configurations (4 methods × 12 M, one pipeline depth) × 3 replicates × ~10-15 min per run
- Per depth: ~24-36 GPU-hours
- Both depths (p=4 and p=8): **~48-72 GPU-hours total**
- Conservative estimate with overhead: **~80-100 GPU-hours**

**Memory requirements:**
- Model size: ~768 hidden dim × 4-8 layers ≈ typical transformer memory profile
- Worst case (M=384, p=8, batch_size=64): Estimate peak GPU memory usage
- Verify no OOM at highest M; if OOM, reduce batch size and document

### 9.4 Data Preparation
- [ ] Generate or cache synthetic dataset (deterministic, fixed random seed)
- [ ] Pre-allocate data to avoid I/O variance during measurement phase
- [ ] Verify dataset size allows 1000+ iterations without repetition during measurement window

---

## 10. DATA COLLECTION & ANALYSIS WORKFLOW

### 10.1 Per-Run Output Format

**CSV structure (one row per run):**
```
run_id,method,pipeline_depth,num_microbatches,replicate_id,
wall_clock_time_sec,iterations_completed,throughput_samples_per_sec,
gpu_peak_memory_mb,iteration_std_dev_ms,bubble_ratio_estimate,
timestamp,notes
```

**Example row:**
```
001,1F1B,4,8,1,125.3,750,19.2,8450,2.3,0.28,2026-10-04T10:30:00,baseline
```

### 10.2 Summary Statistics Table

**Per configuration (averaged across 3 replicates):**
```
method | pipeline_depth | num_microbatches | throughput_mean | throughput_std | throughput_cv | 
       |                |                  | bubble_ratio    | memory_peak_mb | notes
```

### 10.3 Analysis Workflow

**Step 1: Data Quality Check**
- Identify any failed runs (no data, crash, OOM)
- Flag outliers per configuration (|value - median| > 3σ) for inspection
- Verify CV < 5% per configuration; if CV > 10%, mark for potential replication

**Step 2: Descriptive Visualization**
1. **Line plot:** Throughput vs. M, separate lines per method, separate panels per pipeline depth
   - X-axis: M (linear or log scale)
   - Y-axis: Throughput (normalized scheme B: bubble ratio, or scheme C: speedup)
   - Error bars: ±1σ across replicates
   
2. **Heatmap:** Throughput matrix [method × M], separate for p=4 and p=8
   - Color intensity: throughput value
   - Cells: method/M combinations

3. **Box plot:** Throughput distribution per method, collapsed across all M values
   - Shows method ranking and variance

**Step 3: Statistical Hypothesis Testing**
1. Run two-way ANOVA per pipeline depth: Method × Microbatches
2. Extract slope coefficients for linear regression (throughput vs. log₂(M))
3. Conduct slope significance tests (H2, H3 tests as defined in Section 5.3)
4. Calculate pairwise comparisons (Tukey HSD) for method pairs

**Step 4: Report Quantitative Metrics**
- Table of all validation criteria from Section 6.2 (Criterion 1-5): Pass/Fail status
- Slope summary table (all methods, both depths)
- Speedup table (ZB-2p vs. 1F1B, ZB-2p vs. 1F1B-I, ZB-2p vs. ZB-1p) at representative M values

**Step 5: Sensitivity & Robustness Analysis**
- Check for Method × Depth interaction (three-way ANOVA)
- If interaction significant: Identify specific method-depth combinations that deviate
- Plot throughput ratio (p=8 / p=4) per method: should be relatively uniform if methods scale consistently

### 10.4 Final Output Deliverables

1. **Main findings document** (~5-10 pages):
   - Summary of experiment design and execution
   - Key visualizations (line plots, heatmaps)
   - Quantitative results table
   - Hypothesis test outcomes (H1, H2, H3)

2. **Detailed data appendix**:
   - Full raw data CSV (all 288 runs)
   - Per-method summary statistics
   - Statistical test outputs (ANOVA table, regression coefficients with CI)

3. **Reproducibility information**:
   - Exact software versions (Python, PyTorch, cuDNN, NCCL)
   - Codebase commit hash
   - Hardware specifications
   - Experiment runtime dates/times
   - Random seeds used

---

## 11. VALIDATION CRITERIA FOR EXPERIMENT SUCCESS

The experiment design is considered **successfully executed and validated** if:

### 11.1 Execution Completeness
- [ ] ≥95% of 288 configurations complete successfully (≤14 failures acceptable)
- [ ] No configuration has CV > 10% (allow ≤5% of configs with 5-10% CV)
- [ ] All three replicates available for ≥90% of configurations

### 11.2 Statistical Significance
- [ ] Two-way ANOVA shows significant effect of Method: p < 0.01 (strong evidence methods differ)
- [ ] Two-way ANOVA shows significant effect of Microbatches: p < 0.05 (M scaling is real)
- [ ] At least one method × M interaction term: p < 0.05 (confirms differential scaling by method)

### 11.3 Hypothesis Validation
- [ ] **H1 (ZB-2p efficiency at low M):** Speedup ≥ 1.3× over 1F1B at M=p in ≥90% of cases
- [ ] **H2 (slope positivity):** 1F1B, 1F1B-I, ZB-1p slopes all significantly > 0 (p < 0.05)
- [ ] **H3 (ZB-2p flatness):** ZB-2p slope not significantly ≠ 0 (p > 0.05) or |slope| < 10% of others' mean slope

### 11.4 Robustness & Consistency
- [ ] Results are **consistent across pipeline depths:** Method rankings (1F1B < 1F1B-I < ZB-1p < ZB-2p in throughput) hold for both p=4 and p=8
- [ ] Method × Depth interaction is **not significant** for ZB-2p (p > 0.10), confirming depth independence
- [ ] Throughput ordering preserved across M range: If ZB-2p > ZB-1p at M=p, this holds at M=high

### 11.5 Data Quality
- [ ] Bubble ratio estimates are **physically plausible** (0 < bubble_ratio < 0.8)
- [ ] Memory peak usage is **consistent across methods** at same (p, M) (±10% variation expected)
- [ ] Iteration time variance is low (std dev of per-iteration times < 5% of mean iteration time)

### 11.6 Practical Significance
- [ ] ZB-2p throughput benefit is **practically meaningful** (>20% speedup over 1F1B at low M relevant to users)
- [ ] Throughput differences are **clearly distinguishable** (not marginal, >10% apart for methods)

---

## 12. FINAL EXPERIMENT SUMMARY

| Aspect | Specification |
|--------|---------------|
| **Total Configurations** | 96 (4 methods × 12 M values × 2 pipeline depths) |
| **Replicates per Config** | 3 |
| **Total Runs** | 288 |
| **Estimated Runtime** | 48-100 GPU-hours (depending on hardware and model size) |
| **Primary Metric** | Throughput (samples/second), normalized by bubble ratio |
| **Key Distinguisher** | ZB-2p slope near zero vs. others' positive slopes |
| **Statistical Test** | Two-way ANOVA + linear regression slope hypothesis tests |
| **Success Criteria** | All five criteria in Section 11 satisfied |
| **Deliverables** | Main findings document, data appendix, reproducibility info |
