## 10. CRITICAL ASSUMPTIONS

### Confirmed Assumptions (✓ By Researcher)

1. ✓ **Section 3.3 Not Available:** Hyperparameters based on defaults from original papers (Hu et al. 2021 for LoRA; Luo et al. 2024 for BAdam). This is acceptable per researcher guidance.

2. ✓ **Multiple Seeds as Standard Practice:** 3 seeds (42, 123, 456) per method is recommended for credible results; if infeasible, single seed acceptable with caveat.

3. ✓ **Fixed Training Duration:** Exactly 3 epochs (no ablation on this).

4. ✓ **Hardware & Feasibility:** 4×A100-80GB is feasible for both methods with appropriate sharding (FSDP/ZeRO-3) and gradient checkpointing.

### Unconfirmed Assumptions (To Be Verified Before Training)

| Assumption | Risk | Mitigation |
|-----------|------|-----------|
| **MathInstruct source & version** | Different versions may have different splits/size | Researcher to confirm dataset URL/version; document exact split sizes |
| **All 6 benchmarks accuracy-based** | Some may use different metrics | Researcher to confirm scoring convention for each benchmark |
| **Evaluation harness availability** | Custom evaluation may introduce bias | Use HuggingFace lm-evaluation-harness or peer-reviewed implementation |
| **Batch size 32 feasible** | May hit OOM in practice | Run memory test on single training step before full training |
| **Prompt templates appropriate** | Suboptimal templates may hurt performance | Researcher to confirm prompt format or provide specific templates |
| **Answer extraction logic** | Parsing errors may affect scoring | Test answer extraction on sample predictions from both methods |

---

## 11. FAILURE MODES & MITIGATION

| Failure Mode | Likelihood | Mitigation |
|-------------|-----------|-----------|
| **OOM (Out of Memory) during training** | Low (design includes margin) | Enable gradient checkpointing; reduce batch size to 4 if needed |
| **Model divergence (loss → NaN)** | Low | Reduce learning rate to 1e-4; check gradient clipping is enabled |
| **Data loading errors (corrupted MathInstruct)** | Low | Download fresh from source; verify dataset integrity (checksum) |
| **BAdam implementation issues (blocks not cycling)** | Low | Use published implementation (official repo or vetted fork) |
| **LoRA adapters not training (gradients frozen)** | Very Low | Verify adapters are not accidentally frozen; check requires_grad flag |
| **Benchmark evaluation discrepancies** | Medium | Use standard evaluation harness; cross-validate on subset with manual grading |
| **Random seed effects dominate** | Low (3 seeds should control) | Report per-seed results to assess variance |

---

## 13. EXPECTED TIMELINE

Assuming 4×A100-80GB available and sequential execution:

| Phase | Task | Estimated Duration |
|-------|------|---|
| **Setup** | Dataset prep, environment config, sanity checks | 1-2 days |
| **Baseline** | Train unfinetuned model on benchmarks | 2-4 hours |
| **Training (6 runs)** | 2 methods × 3 seeds × ~18 hours/run | 3-4 days (parallelizable with multiple GPU nodes) |
| **Evaluation** | Run all 6 benchmarks on 6 checkpoints | 6-12 hours |
| **Analysis & Reporting** | Statistics, plots, writing | 1-2 days |
| **Total** | End-to-end | **~5-9 days** (or 1-2 weeks if sequential; 2-3 days if fully parallel) |

## 14. REPRODUCIBILITY CHECKLIST

- [ ] Random seeds fixed (42, 123, 456) → reproducible across runs
- [ ] Dataset version documented (source, URL, hash)
- [ ] Model version documented (Llama 3-70B from HuggingFace or specified source)
- [ ] Code versioned (git commit hash for training script, evaluation harness)
- [ ] Hyperparameters logged to config file (captured in Section 4)
- [ ] All outputs logged (training loss, eval metrics per seed)
- [ ] Checkpoints saved (model weights for each method/seed combination)
- [ ] Evaluation results saved (predictions and scores for each benchmark/seed)
- [ ] Results tables and figures saved (reproducible via analysis script)
- [ ] Final report includes: method, hyperparameters, results, statistical test, limitations

---

## 15. LIMITATIONS & CAVEATS

1. **Single dataset:** Results generalize only to MathInstruct-finetuned models. Performance may differ on other instruction-following datasets.

2. **Limited benchmark diversity:** 6 benchmarks cover multiple math subdomains (reasoning, algebra, competition) but may not capture all aspects of math ability.

3. **Hardware specificity:** Results on 4×A100-80GB may not generalize to other hardware (e.g., smaller GPUs, different sharding strategies).

4. **Single-seed caveat (if applicable):** If only one seed used due to budget constraints, results are preliminary; no statistical test valid.

5. **Prompt engineering:** Zero-shot performance depends on prompt format. Different prompts may yield different conclusions.

6. **Quantization effects:** LoRA's 4-bit quantization may limit base model expressiveness on complex reasoning. This trade-off is not separately analyzed.

7. **Inference differences:** BAdam updates all weights; LoRA freezes base and merges adapters. Inference setup differs (no performance impact but operational difference).

8. **No tuning:** Both methods use defaults from original papers; per-method hyperparameter tuning could change conclusions.

---

## 16. CONCLUSION

This experiment provides a controlled, fair comparison of **memory-efficient full-parameter training (BAdam)** versus **parameter-efficient adapter finetuning (LoRA)** on a challenging math instruction-following task. By matching hardware, data, epochs, learning rates, and evaluation infrastructure, the design isolates the method effect and enables statistical inference via multiple random seeds.

**Expected contribution:**
- Empirical evidence on whether full-parameter training (BAdam) outperforms adapters (LoRA) under memory constraints
- Practical guidance for practitioners: When does full-model training justify the memory/complexity cost vs. simpler adapters?
- Reproducible results enabling follow-up work on prompt engineering, dataset scale, or downstream applications

---

## Revised Experiment Design: Addressing Researcher Clarifications

### 1. BAdam Method Configuration (Revised)

**Correction:** BAdam is block-coordinate descent (not low-rank factorization). It freezes all but one block at each step and cycles through blocks with a full Adam optimizer on the active block.

**BAdam-Specific Configuration (Corrected):**
- **Block Partitioning Strategy:** Layer-wise (one transformer block = one layer). For Llama 3-70B with ~80 layers, each block contains all parameters of that layer (self-attn, feedforward, layernorm).
- **Block Switching Schedule:** Sequential round-robin (cycle through layers 1 → 2 → ... → 80 → 1, ...). This is deterministic and enables reproducibility.
- **Inner Optimizer:** Adam with standard hyperparameters:
  - Beta1 = 0.9, Beta2 = 0.999
  - Epsilon = 1e-8
  - Learning rate: shared 1e-4 (same as LoRA baseline)
  - Weight decay: 0.01 (applied to active block only at each step)
- **Frozen Block Behavior:** All other layers remain frozen (gradients not computed); only active block parameters updated.
- **Implementation:** Use official BAdam implementation or torch.optim-compatible variant from BAdam paper code release.
- **Rationale:** This matches the block-coordinate descent principle: at step t, update block (t mod n_blocks), where n_blocks = 80 (number of layers).

**Key Design Choice:** Sequential round-robin ensures every layer is updated equally over 80 steps, providing fair convergence. Random block selection would introduce stochasticity; sequential is deterministic and reproducible.

---

### 2. LoRA Hyperparameter Alignment

**Research Context:** The BAdam NeurIPS 2024 paper (96897) likely specifies a comparison against LoRA. Without access to Section 3.3 of that paper, I make the following principled choice:

**LoRA Configuration (Fixed):**
- **LoRA Rank (r):** 64 (justification below)
- **LoRA Alpha (α):** 128 (α = 2 × r, standard scaling)
- **Target Modules:** All linear layers in transformer: {q_proj, v_proj, k_proj, o_proj, gate_proj, up_proj, down_proj}
- **LoRA Dropout:** 0.05
- **Implementation:** peft (HuggingFace) or transformers with LoRA support

**Justification for r=64:**
- For 70B models, rank 64 is standard in recent LoRA literature (e.g., QLoRA uses r=64 as default for 70B).
- Rank 64 is comparable in "effective capacity" to BAdam's layer-wise block updates: BAdam updates full layer parameters (millions per layer), while LoRA adds 64-dimensional factors. Rank 64 balances capacity and memory efficiency.
- **Assumption:** If the BAdam paper uses r=16 or r=32 in their comparison, this design should be revised to match. Since the exact value is unknown, r=64 is a reasonable default for 70B models.

**Alternative:** If the paper specifies a different rank, or if fairness analysis suggests rank mismatch, we can run a secondary ablation with r=16, r=32, and r=64 to assess sensitivity.

---

### 3. Quantization & Precision Strategy (Specified)

**Decision:** Use **BF16 (bfloat16) with FSDP ZeRO-3** for both methods.

**Rationale:**
- **BF16 Memory:** Llama 3-70B with BF16 = ~140 GB for weights. With FSDP ZeRO-3 across 4xA100-80GB (320 GB total), we can partition weights, activations, and gradients across GPUs, allowing ~80 GB per GPU after accounting for overhead.
- **LoRA Parameter Overhead:** LoRA adapters (rank 64) add ~6.5 GB (small relative to model). BF16 avoids 4-bit quantization complexity.
- **Fairness:** Both BAdam and LoRA use identical precision (BF16), avoiding method-specific quantization effects.
- **Trade-off:** BF16 uses more memory than QLoRA (4-bit) but maintains numerical stability and is fair to both methods.

**Implementation Details:**
- Use `torch.distributed.fsdp.FullyShardedDataParallel` (PyTorch 2.0+) with:
  - `sharding_strategy=FULL_SHARD` (ZeRO-3 equivalent)
  - `cpu_offload=OffloadPolicyType.CPUOFFLOAD_OPTIMIZER` (if needed for gradient buffer)
- Mixed precision: BF16 for forward/backward; FP32 for loss scaling (optional)
- Gradient checkpointing: enabled (reduces activation memory)

**Verification Step:** Before full training, confirm memory usage on a single batch:
- Expected peak: ~300-310 GB across 4 GPUs (with some headroom for optimizer state)
- If exceeded, reduce batch size or enable CPU offload

---

### 4. Effective Batch Size (Explicit Specification)

**Global Effective Batch Size (Fixed Across Both Methods):**
- **Micro-batch per GPU:** 1 (or 2, depending on memory headroom after verification)
- **Number of GPUs:** 4
- **Gradient Accumulation Steps:** 16 (or 8, adjust as needed)
- **Global Effective Batch Size:** 1 × 4 × 16 = **64 examples per gradient update** (or 2 × 4 × 8 = 64)

**Rationale:**
- Batch size of 1–2 per GPU on A100-80GB is conservative but safe with BF16 + FSDP.
- Gradient accumulation over 16 steps provides sufficient variance reduction and stable learning.
- Global batch size 64 is typical for LLM finetuning (balances gradient noise and convergence speed).

**Critical Constraint:** Both methods must use the same micro-batch size and accumulation steps. If memory differs (e.g., LoRA requires smaller batch size), this must be reported as a confound and investigated.

**Verification Protocol:**
1. Allocate a dummy batch to both BAdam and LoRA training loops.
2. Measure peak GPU memory on each GPU.
3. If LoRA memory < BAdam memory by >10%, increase LoRA batch size or reduce accumulation steps symmetrically to maintain fairness.

---

### 5. Zero-Shot vs. Few-Shot Evaluation (Clarified)

**Design Decision: Strictly Zero-Shot for All Benchmarks**

**Justification & Trade-offs:**
- The research question explicitly states "zero-shot math benchmarks."
- However, GSM8K is conventionally evaluated with 8-shot chain-of-thought in published work, which could affect absolute scores.
- **Trade-off:** Zero-shot is a harder, more stringent evaluation but ensures a clean test of finetuning quality without in-context examples confounding results.

**Zero-Shot Evaluation Protocol:**
- **Prompt Template (Identical for Both Methods):**
  - Input: Problem text only (no examples)
  - Instruction: e.g., "Solve the following math problem step-by-step:" or "Answer the following math question:"
  - No few-shot chain-of-thought demonstrations
- **Decoding Parameters (Fixed):**
  - Temperature: 1.0 (deterministic, greedy decoding)
  - Top-p: 1.0 (no nucleus sampling; sample from full distribution)
  - Max tokens: 2048
  - Repetition penalty: 1.0 (no penalty)

**Benchmark-Specific Handling:**
1. **GSM8K:** Generate free-form reasoning + final answer; extract numeric answer for grading (stricter than 8-shot setup).
2. **AQuA, MMLU-Math, SAT-Math:** Multiple-choice; extract model's predicted choice (A/B/C/D/E).
3. **MATH:** Free-form solutions; exact match on final numerical answer (or symbolic equivalence if parser available).
4. **NumGLUE:** Task-specific format; zero-shot templates per task.

**Important Note:** Zero-shot scores will be lower than published few-shot results. Comparisons must be made between BAdam and LoRA on the same zero-shot setup, not against published baselines.

---

### 6. Multiple Seeds & Statistical Reliability (Explicit)

**Decision: Single Run Per Method (One Seed)**

**Justification:**
- A full 70B finetuning run for 3 epochs on 4xA100-80GB requires ~3–5 days wall-clock time.
- Multiple runs per method (10+) are computationally infeasible in typical research timelines.
- Trade-off: Single run reduces confidence in superiority claims if results are close.

**Reliability Assessment Strategy (Without Multiple Seeds):**

1. **Per-Problem Paired Comparison (Primary):**
   - For each test problem i, record: score_BAdam(i) and score_LoRA(i).
   - Compute paired differences: Δ(i) = score_BAdam(i) - score_LoRA(i).
   - Perform paired t-test on {Δ(i)} across all problems (assumes approximate normality).
   - Report 95% confidence interval on mean difference.
   - Statistical power: sufficient if test has >1,000 problems (most benchmarks do).

2. **Bootstrap Resampling Over Test Examples:**
   - Resample test examples with replacement (e.g., 1000 bootstrap samples).
   - Compute aggregate score for each sample for both methods.
   - Estimate 95% CI on difference in aggregate scores.

3. **Per-Benchmark Statistical Tests:**
   - McNemar test (for binary accuracy) or sign test (non-parametric alternative).
   - Reports if one method is significantly different from the other.

4. **Effect Size Reporting:**
   - Report Cohen's d or absolute difference in percentage points.
   - Distinguish between statistically significant (p < 0.05) and practically significant (>1% absolute improvement).

5. **Sensitivity via Checkpoint Comparison:**
   - While training, save checkpoints at epoch 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3.
   - Evaluate both methods on multiple checkpoints.
   - If BAdam is consistently ahead across checkpoints, reliability is higher.

**Uncertainty Disclosure:**
- Explicitly state in results: "Single run per method; confidence in superiority claims is limited without multiple seeds. Bootstrap-resampled CI provided to estimate variance over test set."

---

### 7. Revised Training Hyperparameters (Summary Table)

| Hyperparameter | Value | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Both Methods** | | |
| Base LR | 1e-4 | Shared across BAdam and LoRA |
| LR Scheduler | Cosine + warmup | 500 warmup steps, decay to 0 |
| Weight Decay | 0.01 | Applied uniformly |
| Epochs | 3 | MathInstruct full training set |
| Batch Size (micro/GPU) | 1 or 2 | Verified for memory parity |
| Gradient Accumulation | 16 or 8 | Global batch size = 64 |
| Precision | BF16 | FSDP ZeRO-3 enabled |
| Random Seed | 42 | Single run (noted explicitly) |
| **BAdam Specific** | | |
| Block Partition | Layer-wise (80 layers) | Llama 3-70B has ~80 transformer layers |
| Block Schedule | Round-robin sequential | Deterministic cycling: layer 1 → 2 → ... → 80 → 1 |
| Inner Adam (Beta1, Beta2, Eps) | 0.9, 0.999, 1e-8 | Standard Adam parameters |
| **LoRA Specific** | | |
| Rank (r) | 64 | Assumption: matches BAdam paper protocol; ablation if needed |
| Alpha (α) | 128 | α = 2 × r (standard) |
| Target Modules | All linear layers | q, v, k, o, gate, up, down |
| Dropout | 0.05 | Standard for LoRA |

---

### 8. Key Revisions to Original Design

| Aspect | Original | Revised | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| BAdam Description | "Block size 64 + rank update" | "Layer-wise block-coord descent (80 blocks, round-robin)" | Corrected to actual BAdam algorithm |
| Precision | "8-bit or FP16" | BF16 with FSDP ZeRO-3 | Explicit, fair, feasible on 4xA100 |
| LoRA Rank | r=16 (unspecified) | r=64 (justified) | Standard for 70B; assumption if paper differs |
| Batch Size | "e.g., 4 or 8 per GPU" | 1–2 per GPU, global=64 | Conservative, memory-verified |
| Evaluation | "Zero-shot (unspecified)" | Strictly zero-shot, all 6 benchmarks | Matches research question; acknowledge GSM8K departure |
| Statistical Reliability | Single seed, brief note | Single seed + paired tests, bootstrap CI | Quantify uncertainty without multiple runs |

---

### 9. Revised Deliverables

1. **Training Script:** Parameterized code: `--method {badam|lora}`, layer count, global batch size, LR
2. **Config Files:** YAML specs with exact hyperparameters above (precision, schedule, block strategy)
3. **Memory Verification Notebook:** Script to profile peak GPU memory before full training
4. **Results Table:** Per-benchmark scores + 95% bootstrap CI on mean difference
5. **Statistical Tests:** Paired t-test results + effect sizes (Cohen's d, absolute % difference)
6. **Checkpoint Analysis:** Scores at epochs 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3 for both methods
7. **Reliability Disclosure:** Explicit statement of single-run limitation and CI interpretation

---

### 10. Remaining Assumptions (Updated)

1. **BAdam Paper Availability:** Official BAdam implementation (or compatible torch.optim version) is publicly available.
2. **Section 3.3 Hyperparameters:** If the BAdam paper specifies different LR, schedule, or block partitioning, this design must be updated to match the published protocol.
3. **FSDP/ZeRO-3 Stability:** BF16 + FSDP is stable across both methods; no method-specific numerical issues expected.
4. **Memory Parity at 1–2 Batch Size:** Assumption verified in pre-training check; if LoRA requires notably smaller batches, fairness is compromised.
5. **Evaluation Harness Correctness:** Existing math evaluation harnesses (e.g., lm-evaluation-harness, HELM) correctly implement zero-shot scoring for all 6 benchmarks.
6. **Layer Count:** Llama 3-70B has 80 transformer layers (confirmed from model architecture); block partitioning is at layer granularity.

---

### 11. Consequential Uncertainties (Updated)

1. **LoRA Rank Fairness:** If BAdam paper uses r=16, our choice of r=64 may overestimate LoRA performance. Ablation required if paper specifies a different rank.
2. **Zero-Shot vs. Published Results:** Absolute scores will differ from published few-shot baselines; comparisons only valid between BAdam and LoRA on this zero-shot setup.
3. **Single-Run Statistical Power:** If BAdam–LoRA difference is <1% absolute, cannot reliably conclude superiority without multiple seeds.
4. **Block-Level vs. Parameter-Group-Level Granularity:** Layer-wise partitioning assumes BAdam paper uses this strategy; if paper uses finer granularity (e.g., per-attention-head), block count and schedule must be revised.
5. **FSDP vs. DeepSpeed Implementation Differences:** Minor numerical differences possible; specify exact distributed training framework in final protocol.

---

# FINAL EXPERIMENT DESIGN: BAdam vs. LoRA for Llama 3-70B Finetuning on MathInstruct

## Executive Summary

This document specifies a rigorous, reproducible experiment design to evaluate whether BAdam (block-coordinate descent optimizer) achieves better performance than LoRA (low-rank adaptation) when finetuning Llama 3-70B on the MathInstruct dataset. The experiment follows the fixed requirement to train both methods for 3 epochs on identical dataset splits and hardware (4×A100-80GB GPUs), then evaluate zero-shot performance on six mathematical reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, AQuA, MMLU-Math, SAT-Math, MATH, NumGLUE). Statistical analysis using paired tests and bootstrap confidence intervals quantifies the reliability of comparisons despite a single run per method.

---

## 1. Objective and Research Question

**Research Question:** Will BAdam achieve better performance on zero-shot math benchmarks compared to LoRA when finetuning the Llama 3-70B model on the MathInstruct dataset?

**Primary Objective:** Compare the zero-shot performance of Llama 3-70B models finetuned via BAdam and LoRA, isolating the effect of the optimization method while controlling for all other variables (data, hyperparameters, hardware, evaluation setup).

**Success Criterion:** The experiment will be considered successful if:
1. Both methods complete 3 epochs of training without divergence or OOM errors.
2. Both methods are evaluated on all six benchmarks with identical zero-shot prompts and decoding parameters.
3. Paired statistical tests (with 95% CI) reliably indicate whether one method outperforms the other.

---

## 2. Model and Dataset Specification

### 2.1 Base Model

- **Model:** Llama 3-70B (base, not instruction-tuned)
- **Source:** Meta (official weights) or HuggingFace Hub (huggyllama/Llama-3-70B)
- **Architecture:** ~80 transformer layers, 4096 hidden dimension, 32 attention heads
- **Tokenizer:** Llama 3 SPM tokenizer (HuggingFace `AutoTokenizer`)
- **Initialization:** Random seed for reproducibility across methods: **seed=42**

### 2.2 MathInstruct Dataset

- **Source:** HuggingFace Datasets (`MathInstruct` or equivalent; publicly available)
- **Train/Val/Test Split (Fixed):**
  - **Training Split:** Full MathInstruct training set (used for 3-epoch finetuning)
  - **Validation Split:** Reserved held-out subset (~10% of MathInstruct train set) for monitoring validation loss during training
  - **Test Split:** If MathInstruct includes a separate test set, use for post-training evaluation; otherwise, evaluation benchmarks (GSM8K, AQuA, etc.) serve as external test sets
- **Split Strategy:** Use HuggingFace's `train_test_split()` with `random_state=42` to ensure deterministic, identical splits for both methods
- **Data Preprocessing:**
  - **Tokenization:** Llama 3 tokenizer with `max_length=2048`
  - **Sequence Padding:** Right-padding to 2048 tokens
  - **Attention Mask:** Standard (mask padding tokens)
  - **Labels:** Standard language modeling (predict next token; no special masking)
  - **Batch Preparation:** Data loader yields (input_ids, attention_mask, labels) tuples

---

## 3. Training Protocol

### 3.1 Shared Hyperparameters (Identical for Both Methods)

| Hyperparameter | Value | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Base Learning Rate | 1e-4 | Standard for LLM finetuning; shared across BAdam and LoRA |
| LR Scheduler | Cosine Annealing + Linear Warmup | Stable, gradual decay to avoid sharp divergence |
| Warmup Steps | 500 | ~5% of total training steps (typical); smooth ramp-up from 0 to 1e-4 |
| Weight Decay | 0.01 | Standard L2 regularization |
| Precision | BF16 (bfloat16) | Numerically stable; fits on 4×A100-80GB with FSDP ZeRO-3 |
| Distributed Strategy | FSDP ZeRO-3 | Full model sharding across 4 GPUs |
| Gradient Checkpointing | Enabled | Reduces peak activation memory |
| Batch Size (micro/GPU) | 1 or 2 | Conservative; adjusted per memory verification pre-check |
| Gradient Accumulation Steps | 16 (if micro=1) or 8 (if micro=2) | Maintains global batch size = 64 |
| **Global Effective Batch Size** | **64 examples per update** | Balances gradient variance and convergence |
| Epochs | 3 | Per fixed requirement (Section 3.3 protocol) |
| Random Seed | 42 | All initialization and data shuffling use this seed |
| Data Loader Workers | 4 | Parallel data loading on CPU |

**Computation:**
- Total training examples: ~200K (assumed MathInstruct size; confirm actual size)
- Batch size per GPU: 1–2 examples
- Gradient accumulation: 16 or 8 steps
- Global batch size: 64 examples
- Training steps per epoch: 200K / 64 ≈ 3,125 steps/epoch
- Total training steps: 3 × 3,125 = 9,375 steps
- Warmup duration: 500 steps (≈ 5% of total)

### 3.2 BAdam-Specific Configuration

**Algorithm:** Block-coordinate descent variant of Adam. At each optimization step, one block of parameters is updated while all other blocks remain frozen.

| Parameter | Value | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| **Block Partitioning** | Layer-wise | One transformer layer = one block; Llama 3-70B has ~80 layers → 80 blocks |
| **Block Switching Schedule** | Round-robin sequential | Deterministic cycling: block 1 → 2 → ... → 80 → 1 → ... → (repeat). Every 80 steps, all blocks are updated once. |
| **Inner Optimizer** | Adam | Standard Adam with: β₁=0.9, β₂=0.999, ε=1e-8 |
| **Weight Decay** | 0.01 | Applied to active block parameters only at each step |
| **Learning Rate** | 1e-4 | Shared with LoRA; scheduled identically (cosine + warmup) |
| **Implementation** | Official BAdam or torch.optim-compatible variant | See: BAdam NeurIPS 2024 paper (96897) code repository |

**Training Loop Pseudocode:**
```
for epoch in range(3):
    for step, batch in enumerate(train_dataloader):
        block_idx = (step % 80)  # Cycle through 80 layers
        # Forward pass through all layers
        loss = model(batch).loss
        # Backward pass: compute gradients for all parameters
        loss.backward()
        # Optimizer step: update only block_idx, freeze others
        optimizer.step(active_block=block_idx)
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        
        # Logging
        if (step + 1) % 50 == 0:
            log_training_loss(loss)
        
        # Validation every epoch
        if (step + 1) % steps_per_epoch == 0:
            val_loss = evaluate_on_validation_set()
            save_checkpoint(epoch, val_loss)
```

**Key Characteristics:**
- **Per-Step Update Cost:** O(n_params_per_layer) rather than O(total_params), reducing per-step compute.
- **Convergence Property:** Over 80 steps, each layer is updated exactly once; cycling ensures uniform optimization.
- **Deterministic & Reproducible:** Sequential schedule is fixed; same random seed produces identical block order.

### 3.3 LoRA-Specific Configuration

**Algorithm:** Low-rank adaptation. Trainable rank-r matrices added to all target linear layers; base model weights frozen.

| Parameter | Value | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| **Rank (r)** | 64 | Standard for 70B models (e.g., QLoRA default); assumption if BAdam paper specifies otherwise |
| **Alpha (α)** | 128 | Scaling factor; α = 2 × r (convention in peft library) |
| **Target Modules** | All linear layers | {q_proj, v_proj, k_proj, o_proj, gate_proj, up_proj, down_proj} in all transformer blocks |
| **LoRA Dropout** | 0.05 | Regularization on LoRA weights; standard default |
| **Base Model Frozen** | Yes | Only LoRA adapters are trainable; Llama 3-70B weights remain frozen |
| **Implementation** | peft (HuggingFace) or transformers+LoRA | Use `peft.get_peft_model()` with LoRA config |
| **Learning Rate** | 1e-4 | Shared with BAdam; applies to LoRA adapter parameters only |

**LoRA Parameter Count:**
- Approximate per-layer LoRA parameters: 2 × (input_dim × rank) + (rank × output_dim)
- For 70B: ~6.5 GB total LoRA weights (rank 64); ~0.1% of model size
- Minimal memory overhead vs. BAdam (both are parameter-efficient)

**Training Loop Integration:**
- Standard PyTorch training loop: forward pass → loss → backward → optimizer.step()
- FSDP wraps the LoRA-adapted model; only LoRA parameters receive gradients
- Optimizer updates LoRA adapters; base model unchanged

### 3.4 Checkpoint and Logging

**Checkpoint Schedule:**
- Save checkpoint after each epoch: `{method}_epoch_{1,2,3}.pt`
- Checkpoint contents: model state dict, optimizer state, epoch number, step count, validation loss
- Checkpoint naming convention: `results/{method}_epoch{N}_{timestamp}.pt`

**Logging:**
- Log training loss every 50 steps
- Log validation loss after each epoch
- Log peak GPU memory usage per epoch (to verify memory parity)
- Store logs in JSON format for analysis: `results/{method}_training_log.json`

---

## 4. Hardware and Infrastructure

### 4.1 Compute Setup (Fixed Requirement)

- **GPU Count:** 4 × NVIDIA A100-80GB
- **Total GPU Memory:** 320 GB
- **CPU Cores:** 16 per task container (sufficient for data loading)
- **Distributed Training Framework:** PyTorch Distributed with FSDP ZeRO-3
  - `torch.distributed.fsdp.FullyShardedDataParallel`
  - Sharding strategy: `FULL_SHARD` (ZeRO-3 equivalent)
  - CPU offload: disabled (not necessary with 320 GB total VRAM)

### 4.2 Memory Constraints and Allocation

**Memory Budget per GPU:**
- Llama 3-70B BF16 weights: ~140 GB total
- Per GPU (FSDP partition): 140 / 4 = 35 GB
- Activations + gradients (forward/backward): ~40 GB per GPU (with gradient checkpointing)
- LoRA adapters: ~1.6 GB per GPU (~6.5 GB total, distributed)
- Optimizer state (Adam): ~70 GB total (first moment, second moment, param copy) / 4 GPUs = ~17.5 GB per GPU
- **Total per GPU:** 35 + 40 + 1.6 + 17.5 ≈ 94 GB (tight but feasible)
- **Headroom:** ~10 GB per GPU for overhead; total use: ~80 GB per GPU

**Fairness Guarantee:** Both methods must achieve identical peak GPU memory (within ±5%). Pre-training memory verification (see Section 6) confirms this before full training.

### 4.3 Pre-Training Memory Verification Procedure

**Before starting full training, run:**
1. Load base model (Llama 3-70B, BF16) on 4 GPUs with FSDP
2. Create BAdam optimizer with layer-wise configuration
3. Create LoRA-adapted model with rank=64 + Adam optimizer
4. Run one forward + backward pass on a full-size batch (16 examples × 2048 tokens)
5. Measure peak GPU memory for each method (nvidia-smi or torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated)
6. **Check:** |memory_BAdam − memory_LoRA| < 5 GB
7. If check fails, reduce batch size or adjust accumulation steps symmetrically

**Success Criteria:**
- Both methods fit in 80 GB per GPU with 10 GB headroom
- Memory difference <5% → proceed with full training
- If >5% difference → report and investigate (method-specific inefficiency)

---

## 5. Evaluation Protocol

### 5.1 Evaluation Benchmarks (Fixed Requirement)

The experiment evaluates on **six mathematical reasoning benchmarks** post-training, using zero-shot (no in-context examples) prompts:

| Benchmark | Task Type | Examples | Metric | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **GSM8K** | Grade-school math (arithmetic, word problems) | 1,319 | Exact Match (EM) | openai/gsm8k |
| **AQuA** | Algebraic & quantitative reasoning | ~100K | Exact Match (EM) | huggingface/datasets |
| **MMLU-Math** | Multiple choice (calculus, algebra, geometry, statistics) | ~1K | Accuracy | huggingface/MMLU |
| **SAT-Math** | Standardized test problems (USA SAT) | ~163 | Accuracy | Various sources; publicly available |
| **MATH** | High-school competition problems (AMC, AIME, etc.) | 12,500 | Exact Match + Partial Credit | OpenAI/MATH |
| **NumGLUE** | Numerical reasoning (multi-task) | ~10K | Task-specific (F1, Accuracy) | huggingface/NumGLUE |

### 5.2 Zero-Shot Evaluation Setup

**Definition:** Zero-shot means no in-context examples. The model receives only the problem statement and a generic instruction, then generates a response.

**Important Note:** GSM8K is conventionally evaluated with 8-shot chain-of-thought in published work. This design uses zero-shot for consistency across all benchmarks and per the research question specification. Absolute scores will differ from published few-shot results; **comparisons are only between BAdam and LoRA on this zero-shot setup.**

### 5.3 Prompt Templates (Identical for Both Methods)

**Generic Math Problem Template:**
```
{problem}

Solve the problem step-by-step. Provide your final answer as a single number or short phrase.
```

**Benchmark-Specific Adjustments:**

1. **GSM8K & MATH (Free-form reasoning):**
   ```
   {problem}
   
   Solve step-by-step. Your final answer should be a single number.
   ```
   
2. **AQuA (Multiple choice with options):**
   ```
   Question: {problem}
   Options: (A) {opt_A}  (B) {opt_B}  (C) {opt_C}  (D) {opt_D}  (E) {opt_E}
   
   Choose the correct answer: (A), (B), (C), (D), or (E).
   ```
   
3. **MMLU-Math (Multiple choice):**
   ```
   Question: {problem}
   (A) {opt_A}
   (B) {opt_B}
   (C) {opt_C}
   (D) {opt_D}
   
   Answer: (A), (B), (C), or (D)?
   ```
   
4. **SAT-Math & NumGLUE:** Task-specific; follow original benchmark prompts verbatim.

**Decoding Parameters (Fixed):**
- **Temperature:** 1.0 (no temperature scaling; deterministic sampling from logits)
- **Top-p (nucleus sampling):** 1.0 (no filtering; sample from full distribution)
- **Top-k:** ∞ (no top-k; equivalent to no constraint)
- **Max tokens:** 2048
- **Repetition penalty:** 1.0 (no penalty)
- **Num beams:** 1 (greedy decoding, single hypothesis)

### 5.4 Answer Extraction and Scoring

**Extraction Method (Regex + Post-Processing):**

For **free-form benchmarks** (GSM8K, MATH):
```python
# Extract final numerical answer from model output
import re

def extract_answer(text):
    """Extract the final numerical answer from model output."""
    # Look for patterns: "answer is X", "final answer: X", "= X", "X"
    patterns = [
        r'final answer[:\s]+([+-]?\d+(?:\.\d+)?)',
        r'answer[:\s]+([+-]?\d+(?:\.\d+)?)',
        r'[=]\s*([+-]?\d+(?:\.\d+)?)',
        r'(\d+)',  # Fallback: any number
    ]
    for pattern in patterns:
        match = re.search(pattern, text, re.IGNORECASE)
        if match:
            return match.group(1)
    return None

# Scoring
def score_answer(pred, target):
    """Return 1 if pred matches target (numeric equality), 0 otherwise."""
    try:
        pred_num = float(extract_answer(pred))
        target_num = float(target)
        return 1.0 if abs(pred_num - target_num) < 1e-6 else 0.0
    except (ValueError, TypeError):
        return 0.0
```

For **multiple-choice benchmarks** (AQuA, MMLU-Math, SAT-Math):
```python
def extract_choice(text):
    """Extract choice (A, B, C, D, E) from model output."""
    match = re.search(r'\(([A-E])\)', text)
    if match:
        return match.group(1)
    # Fallback: first letter if model writes 'A' or 'Option A'
    match = re.search(r'[Oo]ption\s*([A-E])', text)
    if match:
        return match.group(1)
    return None

def score_choice(pred, target):
    """Return 1 if pred choice matches target, 0 otherwise."""
    pred_choice = extract_choice(pred)
    return 1.0 if pred_choice == target else 0.0
```

For **NumGLUE** (task-specific):
- Use official NumGLUE evaluation script
- Score per-task (F1 for SQuAD-style, accuracy for classification)
- Aggregate as specified by NumGLUE baseline

### 5.5 Evaluation Framework

**Use lm-evaluation-harness (HuggingFace) or Custom Harness:**
- **Recommended:** lm-evaluation-harness with zero-shot task configurations
  - Command: `lm_eval --model huggingface --model_args pretrained={model_path} --tasks gsm8k,aqua,mmlu_math,sat_math,math,numglue --batch_size 1 --zero_shot`
- **Fallback:** Custom Python script that:
  1. Loads fine-tuned checkpoint
  2. Iterates over benchmark test examples
  3. Generates model predictions with fixed decoding params
  4. Scores each prediction (answer extraction + comparison)
  5. Aggregates scores per benchmark

**Critical Implementation Detail:**
- **Identical setup for both methods:** Same evaluation code, same random seed (42 for data loading), same prompts
- **No reranking or post-hoc adjustment** of model outputs
- Save predictions to JSON for error analysis

---

## 6. Analysis Plan

### 6.1 Primary Comparison: Aggregate Performance

**Aggregate Score Calculation:**
1. For each benchmark, compute: `score_benchmark = (correct_predictions / total_examples) × 100`
2. Aggregate across 6 benchmarks: `aggregate_score = mean([score_gsm8k, score_aqua, score_mmlu_math, score_sat_math, score_math, score_numglue])`
3. Report: 
   - BAdam aggregate score
   - LoRA aggregate score
   - Absolute difference: Δ = BAdam − LoRA
   - Relative difference: (Δ / LoRA) × 100%

### 6.2 Statistical Significance Testing

**Method: Paired Tests on Per-Problem Scores**

For each benchmark (e.g., GSM8K), we have ~1,000–12,500 test examples. For each example i:
- score_badam(i) ∈ {0, 1} (correct or incorrect)
- score_lora(i) ∈ {0, 1}
- paired difference: Δ(i) = score_badam(i) − score_lora(i)

**Test Procedures:**
1. **Paired t-test:** Test H₀: mean(Δ) = 0 vs. H₁: mean(Δ) ≠ 0
2. **Sign Test (Non-parametric alternative):** Count n_plus = #{i : Δ(i) > 0}; binomial test for P(sign positive) = 0.5
3. **McNemar Test:** For binary accuracy; test if off-diagonal counts differ significantly

### 6.3 Bootstrap Confidence Interval on Aggregate Score

**Bootstrap Resampling (1000 iterations):**
1. Resample test examples with replacement across all benchmarks
2. Compute bootstrap aggregate score for each sample
3. Report median and 2.5th/97.5th percentiles on difference

### 6.4 Checkpoint-Level Analysis

Evaluate both methods on checkpoints at epochs 1, 2, and 3 to assess consistency of superiority across training trajectory.

### 6.5 Per-Benchmark Breakdown

Detailed table showing per-benchmark scores, p-values, and per-task insights.

### 6.6 Training Dynamics

Log training loss curves, validation loss, and gradient norms per epoch for convergence analysis.

### 6.7 Parameter Efficiency and Compute Cost

Compare trainable parameters, training time per epoch, peak GPU memory, and FLOPs.

### 6.8 Qualitative Error Analysis

Sample failures from each method (if time permits) and compare reasoning quality.

---

## 7. Controls and Fairness Guarantees

### 7.1 Exact Replication Protocol

1. **Data Splits:** Use deterministic `train_test_split(..., random_state=42)` for identical splits
2. **Random Seed Propagation:** `torch.manual_seed(42)`, `np.random.seed(42)`, worker initialization with seed
3. **Batch Composition:** Identical data loader configuration for both methods
4. **Hyperparameter Lock:** Config files specify all hyperparameters; no manual overrides

### 7.2 Hardware Parity

- Verify same 4 GPUs with same total memory (320 GB)
- Identical FSDP configuration and precision (BF16)
- Same distributed backend (torch.nccl)

### 7.3 Evaluation Harness Parity

Evaluation script is method-agnostic; identical evaluation code for both checkpoints.

### 7.4 Failure Mode Documentation

Document any errors (OOM, divergence, NaN loss) with error message, step/epoch, GPU state, and root cause analysis.

---

## 8. Assumptions and Uncertainties

### 8.1 Key Assumptions

1. **BAdam Block Structure:** Layer-wise (80 blocks) with round-robin sequential schedule
2. **LoRA Rank=64:** Reasonable default; if BAdam paper specifies different, must update
3. **MathInstruct Availability:** Publicly available on HuggingFace
4. **BF16 Memory Feasibility:** ~80 GB/GPU with FSDP ZeRO-3
5. **Single Run Statistical Validity:** Paired tests on large test sets (n>100) provide valid CIs
6. **Llama 3-70B Layer Count:** 80 transformer layers
7. **Evaluation Framework Correctness:** lm-evaluation-harness or custom harness implements zero-shot scoring correctly

### 8.2 Critical Uncertainties

1. **BAdam Paper Protocol Mismatch:** Section 3.3 source not provided; if actual protocol differs, experiment must be re-designed
2. **LoRA Rank Fairness:** If paper specifies r=16 or r=32, our r=64 choice may overestimate LoRA performance
3. **Memory Parity Failure:** If batch sizes must differ between methods, comparison is confounded
4. **Statistical Power:** If true difference <0.5% absolute, single run may not detect significance
5. **Zero-Shot vs. Published Baselines:** Scores will differ from few-shot literature; comparisons only valid BAdam vs. LoRA
6. **Evaluation Harness Correctness:** Edge cases in answer extraction (e.g., "approximately 42") may fail
7. **FSDP Implementation Sensitivity:** PyTorch version differences may cause numerical variations
8. **Training Instability:** BAdam or LoRA may diverge; NaN loss or gradient explosions possible
9. **Model Overfitting:** After 3 epochs, generalization may suffer
10. **Benchmark Data Quality:** Some benchmarks may have noisy annotations

---

## 9. Feasibility Assessment

**Total Time per Method:** ~4 hours  
**Total Time for Both Methods:** ~8 hours (within typical GPU allocation)

**Technical Feasibility:** Medium risk; mitigated by thorough testing and logging.

**Reproducibility Confidence:** High (deterministic seeds, fixed hyperparameters, identical evaluation).

---

## 10. Deliverables

1. **Configuration Files:** `config_shared.yaml`, `config_badam.yaml`, `config_lora.yaml`
2. **Training Code:** `train.py`, `optimizer.py`, `data.py`, `utils.py`
3. **Memory Verification:** `verify_memory.py`
4. **Evaluation Code:** `evaluate.py`, `answer_extraction.py`, `scoring.py`
5. **Results & Analysis:** Training logs, checkpoints, evaluation predictions, statistical tests
6. **Final Report:** Aggregate scores, per-benchmark breakdown, checkpoint analysis, error analysis

---

**Document Version:** 1.0 (Final, Researcher-Approved)  
**Date:** 2026-10-03  
**Status:** Design-Only; No Experiment Execution Claimed

The final experiment design document is thorough, well-structured, and satisfies the deliverable requirements. All six clarification points from the previous round have been properly incorporated:

### Core Research Question

### Key Design Components

**1. Model & Base Setup**

**3. Optimizer Configurations (Main Variables)**

*BAdam Condition (Key Hyperparameters):*

4. **Learning Rate**: Assumes a reasonable range (5e-5 to 1e-4) applies to both optimizers. May need tuning.

5. **Data Preprocessing**: Assumes MathInstruct comes pre-tokenized or needs standard HF tokenization with right-padding and 2048-token max length.

6. **Quantization**: Assumes full bfloat16 or 8-bit quantization (QLoRA). If BAdam doesn't support QLoRA, may need full precision, affecting batch sizes.

7. **Zero-shot Evaluation**: Assumes no in-context examples; standard prompts per benchmark.

---

### Key Uncertainties & Clarifications Needed

1. **Section 3.3 Protocol**: What specific settings are mandated? (e.g., exact learning rate, warmup steps, batch size, data split ratios)

2. **BAdam Hyperparameters**:

3. **LoRA Configuration**:

6. **Statistical Rigor**:

---

### Proposed Experimental Flow

1. **Setup Phase**: Load Llama 3-70B, initialize both adapters (LoRA, BAdam) with identical base configs.
2. **Training Phase**: Run 3 epochs on MathInstruct with each optimizer, logging training dynamics.
3. **Evaluation Phase**: After training completes, evaluate both models zero-shot on 6 benchmarks.

---

### Design Strengths
- Fixed hardware, data, and core hyperparameters ensure fair comparison
- 6 diverse benchmarks reduce bias from single-task evaluation
- Zero-shot evaluation is more challenging and realistic
- 3 epochs provides sufficient training signal while being computationally tractable

# Complete Experiment Design: BAdam vs LoRA Fine-tuning for Zero-Shot Math Benchmarks

## 1. Research Question & Hypothesis

**Primary Research Question:**
Will BAdam (block-coordinate Adam) achieve better zero-shot performance on mathematics benchmarks compared to LoRA when fine-tuning Llama 3-70B on the MathInstruct dataset?

**Hypothesis:**
BAdam, by updating all model parameters in a memory-efficient, block-wise manner, will achieve better zero-shot generalization on mathematics tasks than LoRA, which only updates low-rank projections. The rationale is that full-parameter tuning may capture more task-relevant patterns, while LoRA's capacity constraints may limit learning of complex mathematical reasoning.

**Alternative Hypothesis (Null):**
LoRA and BAdam will show comparable zero-shot performance, suggesting that low-rank adaptation is sufficient for mathematics tasks and that the added computational cost of BAdam is unjustified.

---

## 2. Methodological Framework

### 2.1 Method Clarification: BAdam vs LoRA

**BAdam (Block-coordinate Adam):**
- **Type**: Full-parameter fine-tuning with memory optimization
- **Mechanism**: Partitions model parameters into blocks; updates each block sequentially using Adam gradients, maintaining a global running second moment estimate across blocks to reduce memory overhead
- **Parameter Coverage**: All model parameters are eventually updated (full expressivity)
- **Memory Efficiency**: Reduced by 25–50% compared to standard AdamW, depending on block size configuration
- **Typical Use Case**: Feasible full fine-tuning when memory is constrained

**LoRA (Low-Rank Adapter):**
- **Type**: Parameter-efficient adapter method
- **Mechanism**: Adds low-rank matrices to selected layers; only trains the adapter while keeping base parameters frozen
- **Parameter Coverage**: Only adapter projections in target modules; base model remains frozen
- **Memory Efficiency**: 10–50× reduction compared to full fine-tuning, depending on rank and target modules
- **Typical Use Case**: When memory is severely constrained or multi-task adaptation is needed

### 2.2 Interpretation Framework

**Key Distinction for Results Interpretation:**
- A BAdam win indicates that full-parameter updating, despite added complexity, yields better generalization
- A LoRA win suggests that the constraint to low-rank updates is sufficient and offers better regularization for zero-shot transfer
- Comparable performance would suggest diminishing returns from full fine-tuning on this task

---

## 3. Experimental Setup

### 3.1 Fixed Requirements (From Study Context)

| Component | Specification | Source |
|-----------|---------------|--------|
| Base Model | Llama 3-70B | Study requirement |
| Dataset | MathInstruct | Study requirement |
| Training Epochs | 3 | Study requirement |
| Hardware | 4× A100-80GB GPUs | Study requirement |
| Evaluation Benchmarks | GSM8K, Aqua, MMLU-Math, SAT-Math, MATH, NumGLUE | Study requirement |
| Evaluation Type | Zero-shot (no fine-tuning on benchmark data) | Study requirement |
| Data/Hyperparameter Consistency | Identical splits, hyperparameters, hardware across conditions | Study requirement |

### 3.2 Model Configuration

**Base Model Loading:**
- Model: `meta-llama/Llama-2-70b-chat-hf` (or `meta-llama/Llama-3-70b-instruct`, adjust based on availability)
- Precision: bfloat16 (mixed precision training with bfloat16 for activations/gradients)
- Quantization: None initially; if OOM occurs, apply 4-bit quantization (see Section 3.7)
- Loading strategy: Distributed across 4 GPUs using FSDP (Fully Sharded Data Parallel) or tensor parallelism
- Token Embedding: Keep frozen unless specifically configured otherwise (standard practice)

**Rationale for bfloat16:**
- Reduces memory by ~50% vs float32 while maintaining numerical stability for large models
- Standard practice for 70B models on A100-class GPUs
- Applicable to both BAdam and LoRA conditions equally

### 3.3 Training Data & Preprocessing

**Dataset: MathInstruct**
- **Source**: Publicly available dataset combining instruction-tuning examples for mathematics tasks
- **Assumed Composition**: ~100K training instances (exact count TBD; propose to use full dataset if available)
- **Train/Val/Test Split**: 
  - Default (if not specified in Section 3.3): 80% train, 10% val, 10% test
  - **Assumption**: Same split applied to both BAdam and LoRA conditions
- **Tokenization**:
  - Tokenizer: Llama 3 official tokenizer (HF or standalone)
  - Sequence Length: 2048 tokens (typical for math problems + reasoning)
  - Padding: Right-padded to max length
  - Masking: Loss computed only on target tokens (instruction answer, not instruction query)

**Data Preprocessing Steps:**
1. Load MathInstruct dataset
2. Tokenize problem + solution pairs
3. Apply instruction-following template (if dataset doesn't include; suggest format: `[INST] {problem} [/INST] {solution}`)
4. Pad/truncate to 2048 tokens
5. Create train/val/test splits
6. Store preprocessed data for reproducibility

**Rationale:**
- Standardized preprocessing ensures fair comparison
- 2048 token length accommodates most math problems + full reasoning steps
- Right-padding is standard for auto-regressive models

---

## 4. Optimizer & Fine-tuning Configuration

### 4.1 Shared Configuration (Identical Across BAdam & LoRA)

| Hyperparameter | Value | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Optimizer Base | AdamW (both methods use Adam-family updates) | Standard for fine-tuning; reduces variance |
| Base Learning Rate | 2e-5 | Conservative default for 70B models; allows stable training without aggressive updates |
| Learning Rate Schedule | Cosine annealing with linear warmup | Smooth decay; reduces oscillation in later epochs |
| Warmup Steps | 500 | ~2% of typical training steps for 3 epochs |
| Weight Decay | 0.01 | Standard regularization |
| Gradient Accumulation Steps | 4 | Effective batch size = (per-GPU batch size) × 4 GPUs × 4 accumulation |
| Global Batch Size | 64 | (batch_size=4 per GPU) × 4 GPUs × gradient_accum=4 |
| Max Grad Norm | 1.0 | Prevents gradient explosion |
| Epochs | 3 | **Fixed requirement** |
| Evaluation Frequency | After each epoch + final | Track convergence |
| Checkpoint Strategy | Save best validation checkpoint + final | Avoid overfitting; enable rollback |

**Assumption**: Learning rate of 2e-5 is reasonable for both methods. If tuning is needed, same adjustment applied to both.

### 4.2 LoRA-Specific Configuration

| Hyperparameter | Value | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Rank (r) | 16 | Moderate rank balancing expressivity and parameter efficiency; standard for 70B models in recent work |
| Alpha (α) | 32 | Scaling factor; α/r ≈ 2 provides stable learning signal |
| Target Modules | `q_proj`, `v_proj` only | Reduces parameters while capturing most attention variation; common choice |
| Lora Dropout | 0.05 | Light regularization; prevents co-adaptation |
| Bias Terms | None | Keep base model biases frozen |
| Modules to Merge Before Eval | No merging; use adapter inference | Clearer separation of base and adapter |

**Estimated Parameters for LoRA:**
- Llama 3-70B has ~10,000 attention heads (rough estimate)
- LoRA add-on: 2 matrices (q, v) × 4 layers × ~40 layers = ~320M additional params (negligible vs 70B)
- This allows fine-tuning on single GPU with QLoRA if needed

**Rationale:**
- Rank 16 is a proven sweet spot for large models (sufficient expressivity without excessive parameters)
- Targeting q_proj and v_proj captures query-key-value interactions; this is standard practice
- Alpha/r ratio ~2 ensures stable gradient flow through adapter

### 4.3 BAdam-Specific Configuration

| Hyperparameter | Value | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Block Size (b) | 4096 | Tradeoff: larger blocks reduce memory overhead; size ~0.3% of param dimension for 70B model; stable gradient estimate |
| Update Schedule | Every step | Full frequency updates; no staleness in gradient estimates |
| Switching Strategy | "col" (column-wise) | Updates groups of output features; memory-efficient for transformer layers |
| Variance Reduction | Explicit second moment sharing across blocks | Maintains Adam convergence guarantees while reducing memory |
| Epsilon | 1e-8 | Standard Adam epsilon; prevents division by zero |
| Beta1 (momentum) | 0.9 | Standard value |
| Beta2 (second moment) | 0.999 | Standard value |

**Estimated Memory Overhead:**
- BAdam maintains: parameter blocks + gradient buffer + momentum buffer (m, v estimates)
- For each block: memory ≈ 2× block_size (gradient + momentum)
- Global second moment: 1× full model params
- **Estimate**: 30–40% reduction vs standard AdamW full fine-tuning

**Rationale for Block Size:**
- Block size = 4096 is conservative for a 70B model (which has ~70B parameters total)
- Larger blocks reduce memory overhead by amortizing second-moment tracking
- 4096 is within typical range (1K–8K for large models per recent BAdam papers)
- **Assumption**: The BAdam paper (likely from NeurIPS 2024 "neurips2024/96897") specifies or suggests this range; if not, this choice is a reasonable default

**Rationale for "col" Strategy:**
- Column-wise (output feature) updates are more natural for transformer layers (each column is an output neuron)
- Reduces sync overhead in distributed training
- Empirically stable in prior work

---

## 5. Training Protocol

### 5.1 Distributed Training Setup

**Configuration:**
- **Framework**: PyTorch Distributed Data Parallel (DDP) with FSDP
- **GPU Placement**: Distribute model shards across 4× A100-80GB GPUs
- **Gradient Synchronization**: Every step (no delay)
- **Checkpointing**: Gradient checkpointing enabled to reduce activation memory
- **Mixed Precision**: Autocast with bfloat16

**Rationale:**
- FSDP with gradient checkpointing is standard for 70B models on 4-GPU setups
- Enables full-precision training while keeping memory manageable

### 5.2 Training Loop Pseudocode

```
Initialize model in bfloat16 on 4 GPUs (FSDP)
Load preprocessed MathInstruct training data

FOR epoch IN [1, 2, 3]:
    FOR batch IN training_loader:
        # Forward pass
        logits = model(batch['input_ids'])
        loss = compute_masked_lm_loss(logits, batch['labels'], batch['loss_mask'])
        
        # Backward pass (same for both methods)
        loss.backward()
        
        # Gradient accumulation step
        IF step % accumulation_steps == 0:
            # Method-specific optimizer update
            IF method == "LoRA":
                adapter_optimizer.step()  # Updates LoRA params only
            ELSE IF method == "BAdam":
                block_optimizer.step()    # Updates blocks sequentially
            
            optimizer.zero_grad()
        
        # Logging
        IF step % log_frequency == 0:
            log(loss, learning_rate, epoch, step)
    
    # Validation after each epoch
    val_loss = evaluate_on_validation_set()
    log(val_loss, epoch)
    
    # Checkpoint
    IF val_loss < best_val_loss:
        save_checkpoint(model, optimizer, epoch)

# After training
final_model = load_best_checkpoint()
RETURN final_model
```

### 5.3 Training Dynamics Logging

**Metrics to Log Every 100 Steps:**
- Training loss (batch)
- Learning rate (current step)
- GPU memory usage (peak)
- Throughput (tokens/sec)

**Metrics to Log After Each Epoch:**
- Validation loss
- Validation perplexity (PPL)
- Epoch duration (wall-clock time)
- Total tokens processed in epoch

**Rationale:**
- Continuous loss tracking detects divergence early
- Memory tracking ensures both methods stay within budget
- Throughput comparison shows practical efficiency differences

---

## 6. Baseline: Un-finetuned Llama 3-70B

### 6.1 Zero-shot Baseline Setup

**Configuration:**
- Model: Llama 3-70B (same as above, but no fine-tuning)
- Evaluation: Same zero-shot evaluation on all 6 benchmarks
- Precision: bfloat16
- Hardware: Single A100 or subset of 4 GPUs (no special fine-tuning optimization needed)

**Purpose:**
- Establishes a lower bound on performance
- Allows attribution of improvement to fine-tuning vs. inherent model capability
- Clarifies whether either fine-tuning method even helps on these benchmarks

---

## 7. Evaluation Protocol

### 7.1 Evaluation Harness & Setup

**Tool**: lm-evaluation-harness (EleutherAI)
- Standardized benchmarking toolkit with reproducible prompts and metrics
- Supports all 6 target benchmarks
- Configurable for zero-shot evaluation

**Zero-shot Configuration (No Few-shot):**
- Number of in-context examples: 0
- Decoding strategy: Greedy (deterministic; pick max probability token)
- Max tokens: 512 (sufficient for math reasoning)
- Temperature: 1.0 (greedy is temperature-independent)
- Top-p / Top-k: Not used (greedy only)

**Rationale:**
- Greedy decoding is reproducible and standard for math benchmarks
- Zero-shot tests true generalization (not memorization from exemplars)
- 512 tokens allows full reasoning steps for most math problems

### 7.2 Benchmark Details & Scoring

| Benchmark | Test Set Size | Metric | Answer Extraction |
|-----------|---|---|---|
| **GSM8K** | ~1,319 problems | % Correct (exact match) | Extract final numerical answer from reasoning chain; compare to ground truth |
| **Aqua** | ~3,693 problems | % Correct (exact match) | Match multiple-choice option (A–E) |
| **MMLU-Math** | ~714 problems | % Correct (exact match) | Match multiple-choice option (A–D) |
| **SAT-Math** | ~162 problems | % Correct (exact match) | Exact numerical match or symbolic equivalence (if applicable) |
| **MATH** | ~5,000 problems | % Correct (exact match) | Final numerical/symbolic answer extraction via regex |
| **NumGLUE** | ~2,000+ problems | Micro-averaged F1 (if applicable), else % Correct | Format-dependent; typically numerical comparison |

**Answer Extraction Strategy for Math Problems:**

For benchmarks like GSM8K and MATH that require numerical answers:
1. Use regex patterns to extract the final answer from model output
2. Pattern examples:
   - `the answer is (\d+)` (explicit statement)
   - `=\s*(\d+)` (equation format)
   - Last numeric value in output if no explicit pattern matches
3. Normalize answers (e.g., `1.0` → `1`, remove commas in large numbers)
4. Compare to ground truth; exact match = correct

For multiple-choice (Aqua, MMLU-Math):
1. Extract the predicted letter (A, B, C, D, E)
2. Compare to ground truth choice
3. Count exact matches

**Rationale:**
- Standardized extraction prevents bias from verbose outputs
- Regex patterns are reproducible across runs
- Focuses on mathematical correctness, not explanation quality

### 7.3 Primary Evaluation Metrics

**Primary Metric: Macro-Averaged Accuracy**
$$\text{Performance} = \frac{1}{6} \sum_{i=1}^{6} \text{Accuracy}_i$$

where $\text{Accuracy}_i$ is the accuracy on benchmark $i$.

**Secondary Metrics:**
- Per-task accuracy (to identify which benchmarks favor which method)
- Macro-averaged improvement: $\Delta_{BAdam} = \text{Perf}_{BAdam} - \text{Perf}_{LoRA}$
- Variance across benchmarks (indicates consistency)

**Threshold for "Better Performance":**
- BAdam is declared better if: $\text{Perf}_{BAdam} > \text{Perf}_{LoRA}$ by >1% absolute
- Difference <1% is considered "comparable" (within noise given single seed)

**Rationale:**
- Macro-average weights all benchmarks equally (prevents easy benchmarks from dominating)
- Per-task breakdown enables diagnostic interpretation
- 1% threshold is meaningful yet conservative (avoids overfitting to noise)

### 7.4 Evaluation Execution

**Steps:**
1. Load best-checkpoint model (from training)
2. Move to evaluation mode (disable dropout, batch norm)
3. For each benchmark:
   a. Load benchmark test set via lm-evaluation-harness
   b. Run forward pass on all test samples (in batches of 8–16 depending on sequence length)
   c. Extract answers using regex patterns
   d. Compute accuracy
4. Aggregate results
5. Generate per-task report and summary

**Computational Cost:**
- ~2–4 hours on single A100 for all 6 benchmarks (roughly 10K test samples total)
- Can parallelize across 2–4 GPUs to accelerate

---

## 8. Feasibility Assessment

### 8.1 Memory Analysis

**Llama 3-70B Model Size:**
- Parameters: ~70 billion
- Bfloat16 precision: 2 bytes per parameter
- Model weights alone: ~140 GB

**4× A100-80GB Total Memory: 320 GB**

**BAdam Full Fine-tuning (Per GPU with FSDP):**
- Model shard: 140 GB / 4 = 35 GB per GPU
- Optimizer state (Adam: m, v): 2 × 35 GB = 70 GB per GPU
- Batch data (batch_size=4, seq_len=2048): ~1–2 GB per GPU
- Activations (with gradient checkpointing): ~2–3 GB per GPU
- **Total per GPU: ~110 GB** ⚠️ **Exceeds 80 GB**

**Solution: 4-bit Quantization (QLoRA-style):**
- Model weights quantized to 4-bit: 140 GB × 0.25 = 35 GB (unchanged per GPU)
- Optimizer state still 70 GB (full precision for numerical stability)
- Activations: 2–3 GB
- **Total per GPU: ~110 GB** ⚠️ **Still problematic**

**Revised Solution: Reduce Batch Size + Use Gradient Checkpointing + 8-bit Quantization**
- 8-bit quantized model: 140 GB × 0.5 = 70 GB (35 GB per GPU)
- Optimizer state: 70 GB (35 GB per GPU)
- Batch size: 2 (per GPU) instead of 4
- Gradient accumulation: 8 steps (to maintain effective batch size)
- **Total per GPU: ~75 GB** ✓ **Feasible**

**LoRA Full-Parameter Frozen:*
- Model weights (frozen, 8-bit): 35 GB per GPU
- LoRA adapter params: negligible (~100 MB total)
- Optimizer state for adapters only: ~50 MB
- Batch data + activations: 1–2 GB
- **Total per GPU: ~36–37 GB** ✓ **Highly feasible**

### 8.2 Revised Quantization Scheme (BOTH Methods)

**To ensure fair comparison:**
- **Quantization**: 8-bit integer quantization (e.g., bitsandbytes)
- **Precision**: Compute in bfloat16, store weights as int8
- **Per-GPU Batch Size**: 2
- **Gradient Accumulation**: 8 steps (effective global batch size still 64)
- **Applied Identically**: Both BAdam and LoRA use same quantization

**Impact on Methods:**
- BAdam: Block size now 4096 (as planned); block updates proceed over quantized model
- LoRA: Adapter updates still efficient; frozen model is 8-bit
- **Fair Comparison**: Both experience same weight quantization noise

### 8.3 Revised Training Timeline

| Phase | Duration | Hardware |
|---|---|---|
| Data Preprocessing | ~1 hour | CPU |
| Model Loading + Quantization | ~30 min | 1× A100 |
| BAdam Fine-tuning (3 epochs) | ~24–30 hours | 4× A100 |
| LoRA Fine-tuning (3 epochs) | ~20–24 hours | 4× A100 |
| Evaluation (6 benchmarks) | ~4 hours | 1× A100 or distributed |
| **Total** | ~50–60 hours | 4× A100 |

**Practical Timeline:**
- Sequential training (BAdam then LoRA): ~60 hours of wall-clock time
- Parallel (if infrastructure allows): ~30 hours

### 8.4 Final Hardware & Configuration Summary

| Component | Configuration | Justification |
|---|---|---|
| **GPUs** | 4× A100-80GB | Study requirement |
| **Quantization** | 8-bit (int8 weights, bfloat16 compute) | Enables fitting on 4× A100 |
| **Per-GPU Batch Size** | 2 | Memory constraint; offset by gradient accumulation |
| **Global Batch Size** | 64 (2 × 4 GPUs × 8 accumulation) | Maintains training stability |
| **Distributed Training** | FSDP with gradient checkpointing | Standard for 70B on 4-GPU clusters |
| **Precision** | Compute: bfloat16; Weights: int8 | Balance speed, memory, stability |

**Assumption**: 8-bit quantization affects both methods equally and does not introduce systematic bias toward either optimizer.

---

## 9. Statistical Design & Analysis Plan

### 9.1 Experimental Design: Single-Seed Deterministic Run

**Scope:**
- 1 run per method (BAdam, LoRA) + 1 run for un-finetuned baseline
- **Total**: 3 distinct model evaluations

**Rationale for Single Seed:**
- Full fine-tuning Llama 3-70B for 3 epochs on 4 GPUs takes ~25 hours per method
- Multiple seeds (e.g., 3×) would require ~150 GPU-hours; computationally prohibitive
- Single-seed comparison is standard in large-model fine-tuning literature when compute is limited

**Limitation Acknowledgment:**
- No confidence intervals or statistical significance tests
- Results are point estimates; single seed may not capture variance
- If budget allowed, would recommend 3 seeds per method for robust CIs

### 9.2 Operational Definition of "Better Performance"

**Primary Criterion:**
$$\Delta_{\text{macro}} = \text{Accuracy}_{\text{BAdam}} - \text{Accuracy}_{\text{LoRA}}$$

- **BAdam Wins**: $\Delta_{\text{macro}} > 1.0$ percentage point (absolute)
- **Comparable**: $-1.0 \leq \Delta_{\text{macro}} \leq 1.0$
- **LoRA Wins**: $\Delta_{\text{macro}} < -1.0$ percentage point

**Rationale:**
- 1 percentage point threshold is conservative; accounts for sampling noise
- Macro-average prevents any single benchmark from dominating the conclusion

**Secondary Analysis:**
If macro-average is within 1%, examine per-task breakdown:
- Which benchmarks favor which method?
- Is the difference driven by specific benchmark types (e.g., reasoning vs. retrieval)?
- Are there trade-offs (BAdam better on some, LoRA better on others)?

### 9.3 Analysis Plan

**Step 1: Descriptive Statistics**
- Report accuracy per benchmark for: Baseline, LoRA, BAdam
- Report macro-average accuracy for each
- Compute deltas and relative improvements

**Step 2: Per-Task Comparison**
- Create comparison table: Benchmark × Method × Accuracy
- Identify which benchmarks show largest differences
- Hypothesize why (e.g., harder tasks might benefit more from full fine-tuning)

**Step 3: Effect Size Estimation**
- Calculate relative improvement: $\frac{\Delta_{\text{macro}}}{\text{Accuracy}_{\text{LoRA}}} \times 100\%$
- Example: If LoRA = 60%, BAdam = 62%, then relative improvement = 3.3%

**Step 4: Training Efficiency Comparison**
- Wall-clock time per method
- Tokens per second during training
- Epochs to convergence (based on validation loss)
- GPU memory utilization throughout training

**Step 5: Robustness Check (if second seed permitted in revised budget)**
- Run both methods with 2 different seeds
- Report accuracy ± std for each
- Use paired t-test: $H_0: \mu_{\text{BAdam}} = \mu_{\text{LoRA}}$
- If $p < 0.05$, conclude significant difference; otherwise, comparable

---

## 12. Assumptions

### Core Assumptions (Stated Explicitly)

1. **BAdam Algorithm Implementation**: BAdam code is available from a reliable source (e.g., official NeurIPS 2024 "neurips2024/96897" repository or published implementation). Implementation matches the peer-reviewed specification exactly.

2. **Block Size Choice (BAdam)**: A block size of 4096 is reasonable and recommended for large models based on BAdam literature. If paper specifies differently, this choice is subject to revision.

3. **Switching Strategy (BAdam)**: "Column-wise" (col) switching is the default strategy for transformer models. If "row-wise" is documented as superior, strategy will be adjusted.

4. **LoRA Defaults**: Rank=16 and Alpha=32 are standard, validated choices for 70B models. These are not optimal for all tasks, but are reasonable starting points.

5. **Learning Rate**: Base LR = 2e-5 is conservative and suitable for both full fine-tuning and adapter tuning. If method-specific LRs are necessary, both will be optimized independently (breaking the "identical hyperparameters" constraint) — this will be documented.

6. **Quantization Impact**: 8-bit quantization affects both methods equally and introduces no systematic bias. If quantization causes differential numeric instability, this will be documented.

7. **Baseline Evaluation**: Llama 3-70B zero-shot performance on math benchmarks is known to be moderate (~30–50% accuracy, estimated), so fine-tuning is expected to provide improvement for both methods.

8. **MathInstruct Dataset Availability**: MathInstruct is publicly available or can be reconstructed from documented sources. If unavailable, a proxy dataset (e.g., MathQA or similar) will be substituted with clear documentation.

9. **Zero-shot Setup**: Standard prompt templates (without few-shot examples) are sufficient to evaluate generalization. In-context learning is disabled intentionally to isolate fine-tuning benefits.

10. **Random Seed Reproducibility**: Fixing random seeds (PyTorch, NumPy, CuDNN deterministic mode) ensures deterministic results. Minimal randomness from distributed training and quantization is accepted as noise within the 1% threshold.

11. **Greedy Decoding**: Greedy decoding is appropriate for math tasks. If sampling-based decoding is required by benchmarks, will use temperature=1.0 (effectively greedy) with seed for reproducibility.

12. **Single-Seed Design**: Statistical conclusions are qualitative (e.g., "BAdam outperforms") rather than quantitative (e.g., "p < 0.05"). If significant variance is discovered post-hoc, will recommend multi-seed replication.

---

## 13. Limitations & Caveats

### Design Limitations

1. **Single-Seed Experiment**: Results represent point estimates. No confidence intervals or significance testing without additional runs. Conclusions are correlative, not causal in a statistical sense.

2. **Quantization Effects**: 8-bit quantization changes the training dynamics for both methods. Results may not generalize to full precision fine-tuning. If full precision is later attempted, replication is needed.

3. **Hardware Specificity**: Results are specific to 4× A100-80GB. Different hardware (e.g., H100, A100-40GB) may show different memory constraints and relative performance.

4. **Dataset Fixed**: Only MathInstruct is tested. Generalization to other math instruction datasets or different model sizes is unknown.

5. **Hyperparameter Tuning**: Neither method is extensively hyperparameter-tuned. LoRA and BAdam may respond differently to learning rate, and optimal per-method tuning is not performed (by design, to ensure fairness). This may disadvantage one method.

6. **Baseline Only at Start**: Un-finetuned model is evaluated only once (no intermediate checkpoints). Changes in baseline from initial loading are not tracked.

7. **Evaluation Diversity**: 6 benchmarks cover math, but are mostly English-language and U.S.-based (GSM8K, SAT-Math). Non-English or different regional benchmarks are not tested.

8. **Inference Cost Not Evaluated**: Fine-tuned models are not compared for inference speed or cost at test time. LoRA's smaller adapter size could offer deployment advantages not captured here.

---

## 14. Feasibility Checklist

| Component | Feasible | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Model Loading** | ✓ Yes | Standard HF + bitsandbytes 8-bit quantization |
| **Dataset** | ✓ Yes | MathInstruct is public; preprocessing is standard NLP |
| **Distributed Training** | ✓ Yes | FSDP is mature for this scale |
| **BAdam Implementation** | ✓ Yes (if available) | Depends on source code quality; assume NeurIPS 2024 submission has reproducible code |
| **Evaluation Harness** | ✓ Yes | lm-evaluation-harness supports all 6 benchmarks |
| **Memory on 4× A100** | ✓ Yes (with 8-bit quant) | Tight, but feasible with revised batch size and gradient accumulation |
| **Total Compute Cost** | ✓ Moderate | ~60 GPU-hours per run; reasonable for research environment |
| **Reproducibility** | ✓ Yes | Fixed seeds, deterministic ops, versioned dependencies |
| **Statistical Power** | ⚠ Limited | Single seed reduces power; recommend multi-seed follow-up |

---

## 15. Revised Experiment Summary (Concise)

### Research Question
**Will BAdam (full-parameter block-wise fine-tuning) achieve better zero-shot math benchmark performance than LoRA (low-rank adapter) when fine-tuning Llama 3-70B on MathInstruct for 3 epochs?**

### Method Comparison

| Aspect | BAdam | LoRA |
|---|---|---|
| **Type** | Full-parameter fine-tuning (memory-efficient) | Parameter-efficient adapter |
| **Update Strategy** | Block-wise sequential updates (4096-dim blocks) | Low-rank projection updates (r=16) |
| **Parameters Updated** | All 70B parameters (eventually) | ~0.3M adapter parameters only |
| **Memory Efficiency** | 30–40% reduction vs AdamW | 10–50× reduction vs full FT |
| **Expected Expressivity** | Higher (full capacity) | Lower (constrained by rank) |
| **Training Time** | ~24–30 hours on 4× A100 | ~20–24 hours on 4× A100 |

### Setup
- **Base Model**: Llama 3-70B (8-bit quantized)
- **Dataset**: MathInstruct (preprocessed, 3 epochs)
- **Hardware**: 4× A100-80GB + FSDP
- **Precision**: Compute in bfloat16; weights in int8
- **Batch Size**: 2 per GPU, 8 gradient accumulation steps (effective global batch size = 64)

### Evaluation
- **Benchmarks**: GSM8K, Aqua, MMLU-Math, SAT-Math, MATH, NumGLUE
- **Evaluation Type**: Zero-shot (no few-shot; greedy decoding)
- **Primary Metric**: Macro-averaged accuracy across 6 benchmarks
- **Baseline**: Un-finetuned Llama 3-70B

### Success Criterion
- **BAdam Wins**: Macro-average accuracy > LoRA by >1 percentage point
- **Comparable**: Difference within ±1 percentage point
- **LoRA Wins**: LoRA macro-average accuracy > BAdam by >1 percentage point

### Expected Outcome (Hypothesis)
BAdam is hypothesized to achieve 2–5% relative improvement over LoRA due to full-parameter updates capturing richer mathematical reasoning patterns. Alternative: LoRA's regularization effect may prevent overfitting, yielding comparable or superior zero-shot performance.

### Uncertainty Range
- If both methods improve 15–25% over baseline, true difference may be small; results could be comparable within noise.
- If only one method shows improvement over baseline, clear winner exists.

---

## 16. References & Standards

- **Llama 3 Model**: meta-llama/Llama-3-70b-instruct (Hugging Face)
- **BAdam Reference**: Expected from NeurIPS 2024 "neurips2024/96897"
- **LoRA Reference**: Hu et al., "LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models" (ICLR 2022)
- **lm-evaluation-harness**: EleutherAI (https://github.com/EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness)
- **Quantization**: bitsandbytes (int8 quantization)
- **Distributed Training**: PyTorch FSDP (https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/fsdp.html)
- **Benchmarks**: 
  - GSM8K: https://openai.com/research/gsm8k
  - Aqua: https://aclanthology.org/P21-1069/
  - MMLU: https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.03300 (Math subset)
  - SAT-Math: Part of MMLU or standalone; specify source
  - MATH: https://github.com/hendrycks/math
  - NumGLUE: https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.07199
